sections.heading: 0625 against the three qualifications families confuse it with
paragraphs: A large share of the wasted revision we see comes from a student working through the wrong resources. Four qualifications sit close enough together to be mistaken for one another, and the subject name on a school report will not distinguish them. The only reliable identifier is the syllabus code on the statement of entry, which is why it is worth asking the exams officer for that document rather than relying on what a subject teacher mentioned in a parents evening.

Cambridge offers both 0625 and a 9 to 1 graded variant of IGCSE Physics, with the same subject content but a different reporting scale. Pearson Edexcel's International GCSE Physics is a separate qualification with its own specification, its own papers and a different treatment of practical skills. And Cambridge Co-ordinated Sciences is a double award covering biology, chemistry and physics together, with less physics content than 0625 and a different paper structure. A child entered for the double award who revises from 0625 materials will meet topics they will never be examined on.

None of these is harder than the others in any useful sense; they are differently shaped. What matters practically is matching the resources, the past papers and the mark schemes to the code your child is entered for, and understanding which scale the grade will be reported on. Both Cambridge and Pearson publish their specifications and specimen material openly, and we work from those rather than from third-party summaries. We do not supply syllabus documents, past papers or mark schemes ourselves; we cite them and link to the boards.

sections.heading: The six topic areas, and the marks each one quietly costs
paragraphs: The 0625 content divides into six areas: motion, forces and energy; thermal physics; waves; electricity and magnetism; nuclear physics; and space physics. Families tend to assume difficulty is spread evenly across them and that the hardest topic deserves the most hours. The evidence from marked scripts says something different. Marks are lost in clusters, and the clusters are often about presentation and reasoning rather than about the physics itself.

Electricity and magnetism is the area that most often produces a collapse in a mock result, because it is cumulative. A student who is shaky on current in series and parallel branches cannot reason about potential dividers, and cannot then handle induction or the transformer questions that depend on the same picture. Repairing this area is a sequence, not a topic, and it is the clearest case for twice-weekly short sessions rather than one long one.

Motion, forces and energy is where unit prefixes and graph work do the damage. A student who reads a distance-time gradient as a value without checking the axis units can lose every mark in a question they understood perfectly. Thermal physics and waves punish imprecise language, because the command word asks for an explanation and the answer describes. Nuclear and space physics are the two areas most often taught last and revised least, and they are usually the cheapest marks available to a student starting late. A student who has three weeks and wants the largest return should ask which of the six areas their own marked papers keep losing marks in, then start there rather than at the front of the textbook.

sections.heading: Practical physics when the teaching happens on a screen
paragraphs: This is the first question serious parents ask, and it deserves a direct answer. Cambridge assesses practical physics either through Paper 5, a practical test carried out under examination conditions at the centre, or through Paper 6, a written alternative to practical. Both are set and marked by Cambridge, both happen at your child's school, and neither is affected by where tutoring takes place. What a tutor can do is train the skills those papers reward, and most of those skills are recording, analysis and reasoning rather than manipulation of apparatus.

In a live video lesson that training is straightforward and often better than it is in a crowded laboratory. A student reads a scale from an image of a real instrument and states the precision. They tabulate results with units in the column headings, which is where marks are routinely dropped. They plot a graph on paper, photograph it, and have the scale choice, point accuracy and best-fit line marked against the scheme. They write an improvement that names a specific change rather than asking for more accuracy, and they get told why the vague version earns nothing.

What online teaching cannot replace is time holding apparatus. A student entered for the Paper 5 practical test needs laboratory practice, and that comes from school. If your child's centre enters Paper 5 and the school's laboratory time is thin, that is a conversation to have with the department rather than something tutoring can fix. For centres entering Paper 6, the written alternative, screen-based teaching covers essentially the whole assessment, which is why we ask which route the centre has entered before planning anything.

sections.heading: Equations, data and what the exam actually hands your child
paragraphs: Every year families ask whether equations are provided in the examination, and every year someone answers confidently from the wrong syllabus version. Cambridge revises syllabuses on a cycle, and the rules about which relationships a candidate must recall, what appears on any supplied list, and what calculator is permitted belong to the syllabus document for your child's specific series. That document is published openly on cambridgeinternational.org, and the exams officer can confirm which version governs the entry. We will not restate those rules here as though they were fixed.

What is stable is the behaviour that earns marks regardless of what is supplied. Write the relationship before substituting numbers, so a method mark survives an arithmetic slip. Substitute with units attached. Convert prefixes at the point of substitution rather than at the end, where the conversion gets forgotten. Round only in the final line and state the unit. Those four habits recover more marks across a paper than any single topic does, and they are trainable in a fortnight.

The same discipline applies to data in questions. Physics papers frequently supply a value a student assumes they must remember, and supply it in a form that needs converting. Students lose marks by not reading the stem carefully enough to notice. Our marked-script cycle exists largely to surface this class of error, because it is invisible in a lesson where the tutor explains and the student nods, and obvious the moment somebody marks the child's own written attempt against the published scheme.
bullets: Check the syllabus version for your child's series before trusting any equation claim
Write the relationship, substitute with units, convert prefixes at substitution
Round once, in the final line, and always state the unit
Read the stem for supplied data before assuming a value must be recalled

sections.heading: ADEK, the inspection report and what it tells you about physics
paragraphs: Al Ain is part of the Emirate of Abu Dhabi, so its private schools sit with the Department of Education and Knowledge, which supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate. Dubai's KHDA has no jurisdiction here, Sharjah has its own authority, and Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah come under the federal Ministry of Education. The regulator map for UAE private schools is published on u.ae, and families moving between emirates are changing regulator as well as address.

An inspection outcome is useful context and a poor proxy for your child's physics department. A whole-school judgement aggregates every subject and phase; a strong school can have a thin year of separate-science staffing, and a mid-rated school can have an outstanding physics teacher who has run the Extended course for a decade. The questions that actually predict your child's experience are narrower: who teaches Year 11 physics, how many periods a week, whether the centre enters Paper 5 or Paper 6, and whether the syllabus will be finished before the mock.

There is one regulatory point with direct bearing on tutoring. Private tuition in the UAE runs on a permit introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, which per u.ae is granted free of charge for two years, with eligible applicants including registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed individuals, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Those tutoring without a permit from MoHRE are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws. Abu Dhabi's professional-ethics rules also bar school staff from paid private tutoring of students enrolled at their own school, so hiring your child's own physics teacher privately is not available to you.

sections.heading: What physics tuition costs in Al Ain, and what the price does not buy
paragraphs: Three of the six competitor pages we examined for this market publish no price at all, and the two that do quote in US dollars. Al Ain parents pay in dirhams, so the figures here are published AED rates with the source attached to each. These are market rates and not IB Gram's price list. Our own arrangement starts with a free trial lesson and a conversation about how many weeks remain, because the right number of sessions for a student in October and one in April are not the same number.

The bands are consistent across the market. Budget online tutoring sits below AED 150 an hour and generally buys homework supervision; on Extended physics that distinction is real, since checking an answer is not the same as diagnosing why circuit reasoning keeps failing. Qualified subject teaching online clusters between AED 150 and AED 300. Visiting in-home rates run higher because travel is inside them. Specialist IGCSE and A-Level rates start around AED 200 and rise, and premium named tutors are quoted considerably above that. Monthly packages exist too, with published examples around AED 799 for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to AED 1,799 for four two-hour in-home sessions.

What no rate buys is a grade. Any page offering a guaranteed outcome for a price is describing something it cannot deliver, and in this market that pattern appears often enough to be worth naming. What a higher rate should buy is specific: diagnosis against the syllabus, marking against the published scheme, and honesty about the calendar. Set the cost against the context, too. KHDA confirmed in May 2026 that Dubai private school fees would not rise for 2026-27 and Abu Dhabi fee decisions sit with ADEK, but tutoring is an addition to a bill that is already large, which argues for fewer and better-targeted hours.

process.title: Send the paper, not the worry
process.description: The most useful first message contains the mock script or its mark breakdown, the syllabus code from the statement of entry, and the series your child is entered for. That lets us match a tutor to the actual gap rather than to the subject name, and it shortens the diagnostic phase by a session.

process.title: Free trial lesson with a 0625 diagnostic
process.description: The first lesson costs nothing. The tutor works through short items across the six topic areas plus one experimental-method question, and reports which areas need teaching, which need technique work, and which are already secure. You get that in writing rather than as a verbal impression.

process.title: A plan with the components named
process.description: The plan states which papers your child sits, which practical route the centre has entered, the order topics will be taught in, and what gets dropped if there are too few weeks. Where the honest answer is that full coverage is no longer possible, the plan says so.

process.title: Weekly teaching plus marked scripts
process.description: Sessions run in your agreed Gulf Standard Time slot. Between lessons your child sits questions to time and sends the script; the tutor marks it against the published scheme so the lesson is spent on lost marks instead of on topics already understood.

process.title: A practical-skills block before the series
process.description: Paper 5 and Paper 6 carry a fifth of the grade and receive the least attention in most revision plans. We schedule a dedicated block on instrument reading, tabulation, graph plotting and improvement writing, aligned to whichever route your child's centre has entered.

process.title: Change the tutor whenever it is not working
process.description: Physics explanations are personal, and a tutor who lands with one student will not land with every student. Tell us after any lesson and we move you, with no penalty and no requirement to justify the decision. The trial exists so that this happens before money has changed hands.

whyPoints.title: The comparison is on this page, not hidden
whyPoints.description: We have set out the four options a parent in Al Ain is actually weighing, including the free one and the two we do not sell, with published rates attached. If the school clinic or a group class is the right answer for your child, this page should help you reach that conclusion faster.

whyPoints.title: Chosen for teaching 0625, not for being nearby
whyPoints.description: Because lessons run one-to-one over live video, the pool is everyone qualified to teach Extended physics rather than everyone who can reach your district by 18:30. In a city the size of Al Ain, on a narrow specialism, that is the whole of the argument.

whyPoints.title: Marking against the published mark scheme
whyPoints.description: Your child's own scripts are marked question by question with the lost marks named, including the ones lost to units, prefixes and command words. That is a different activity from being told an answer is wrong, and it is where most of the recoverable marks sit.

whyPoints.title: The practical component is planned, not assumed
whyPoints.description: Paper 5 and Paper 6 carry a fifth of the grade. We ask which route the centre has entered before planning, and we say plainly that laboratory time for the practical test has to come from school rather than from a video lesson.

whyPoints.title: Sources cited, not paraphrased
whyPoints.description: Regulator statements on this page come from u.ae, and board rules from Cambridge and Pearson's own published material. We link out rather than reproducing syllabus documents, past papers or mark schemes, which are the boards' copyright and not ours to distribute.

whyPoints.title: No accreditation claims and no invented numbers
whyPoints.description: IB Gram holds no approval from ADEK, KHDA, the Ministry of Education, Cambridge, Pearson or the IB, and claims none. Every AED figure here is attributed to whoever published it, and no outcome on this page is guaranteed, because no honest tutor can guarantee one.

faqs.question: Which practical component will an Al Ain centre enter my child for?
faqs.answer: That is the centre's decision, not yours and not the tutor's. Cambridge offers Paper 5, a practical test carried out under examination conditions, and Paper 6, a written alternative to practical, and a school chooses which route it enters candidates for based on its laboratory capacity and staffing. The statement of entry names the components your child will actually sit, so ask the exams officer for it. The distinction matters for planning, because Paper 6 can be prepared almost entirely through written work while Paper 5 needs genuine laboratory time that only the school can supply.

faqs.question: My son's school runs a free physics clinic. Is a paid tutor still worth it?
faqs.answer: Try the clinic first, properly, for three or four weeks. It is free, it is run by someone who knows the teaching order your child experienced, and it often has very few students in the room. Its limitation is that it answers the questions a student brings, which assumes the student can name what they do not understand. Most cannot; they know the mock felt impossible. If your son returns from the clinic unable to say what changed, the gap is diagnosis rather than access, and that is what one-to-one teaching with marked scripts provides.

faqs.question: Does a small group class work for Extended physics?
faqs.answer: It works well for one specific problem: content that has not been taught yet. A class that has not reached nuclear physics by February genuinely benefits from being taught nuclear physics, and a group rate is cheaper per hour than one-to-one. It works poorly for technique, because the marks a student loses on command words, unit prefixes, graph gradients and missing working are personal to them. Six students in a room lose marks in six different ways, and a group lesson can only address the average. Diagnose first, then choose the format that fits the diagnosis.

faqs.question: How is the 0625 grade split across the papers my child sits?
faqs.answer: The multiple-choice paper carries 30 per cent of the total, the theory paper carries 50 per cent and the practical component carries 20 per cent. Core candidates sit Papers 1 and 3; Extended candidates sit Papers 2 and 4; all candidates sit either Paper 5 or Paper 6. The practical fifth is the share most families under-prepare, because it receives the least class time. Confirm the components, durations and marks for your child's specific series against the syllabus on cambridgeinternational.org, since Cambridge revises syllabuses on a cycle and the version for the entry is the one that governs.

faqs.question: Is Cambridge 0625 the same course as the 9 to 1 graded physics IGCSE?
faqs.answer: The subject content is the same separate-science physics, but the grade is reported on a different scale. Cambridge offers both an A star to G variant and a 9 to 1 variant of IGCSE Physics, and a school chooses which to enter. For revision this rarely matters, since the same past papers and mark schemes apply to the content. For university and equivalency paperwork it does matter, because the certificate states the scale. The syllabus code on the statement of entry tells you which one your child is entered for, and that is the document to check rather than the school report.

faqs.question: Should my daughter take separate physics or Co-ordinated Sciences?
faqs.answer: That decision usually belongs to the school and to the timetable, and it is made before Year 10 rather than during Year 11. What matters once the entry exists is that the revision matches it. Co-ordinated Sciences is a double award covering biology, chemistry and physics together, with less physics content than 0625 and differently structured papers. A student entered for the double award who revises from 0625 resources will spend evenings on material they will never be examined on. Check the syllabus code on the statement of entry before buying any revision resource.

faqs.question: Which topic area should we start with after a weak physics mock?
faqs.answer: Usually electricity and magnetism, and not because it is the hardest. It is the most cumulative. A student unsure about current in series and parallel branches cannot reason about potential dividers, and therefore cannot handle induction or transformer questions either, so one weak foundation shows up across several questions and drags the whole paper down. Rebuilding it is a sequence rather than a single topic, which is why it responds to two short sessions a week rather than one long one. The marked mock script tells us whether that is your child's pattern or a different one.

faqs.question: Can an online tutor prepare my child for the Paper 5 practical test?
faqs.answer: Partly, and we are specific about which parts. The recording, tabulation, graph and analysis skills that carry most of the marks are taught well over live video: reading an instrument to the right precision, putting units in column headings, choosing a sensible scale, drawing a best-fit line and writing a named improvement rather than asking for more accuracy. What a video lesson cannot supply is time holding apparatus. If your child's centre enters Paper 5 and laboratory time at school is thin, raise that with the department, because tutoring cannot substitute for it.

faqs.question: Where do I find out which equations 0625 expects my child to recall?
faqs.answer: In the syllabus document for your child's specific series, published openly on cambridgeinternational.org, and confirmed by the exams officer who made the entry. Cambridge revises syllabuses on a cycle, so a confident answer taken from a forum or an older revision guide can describe a version that no longer applies. Whatever the rules turn out to be, the mark-earning habits are the same: write the relationship before substituting, substitute with units attached, convert prefixes at the point of substitution, and round once in the final line with the unit stated.

faqs.question: Can a student move between Core and Extended physics during Year 11 in Al Ain?
faqs.answer: Tier changes are possible and they are an administrative matter for the centre, bounded by Cambridge's entry and amendment deadlines rather than by anyone's opinion of the student. The practical reality is that the decision has to be made early enough for the entry to be amended, which means the conversation belongs weeks before the final entry date rather than after a disappointing mock. Ask the exams officer what the amendment window is for your child's series, and in the meantime work on the supplement content, because dropping to Core later costs nothing that was learned.

faqs.question: How late can a physics session start for a family in Zakher or Al Towayya?
faqs.answer: For most families in the outer districts, 18:30 Gulf Standard Time is the realistic earliest once the drive home and a meal are done, and plenty of our sessions run later than that. Two caveats are worth stating. Technical material taught after a long school day is retained poorly, so a late slot is usually better spent reviewing a marked script than meeting electromagnetic induction for the first time. And during Ramadan slots can move to post-Iftar timing, which we agree before the month begins rather than renegotiating week by week.

faqs.question: Is a visiting physics tutor in Al Ain better value than an online specialist?
faqs.answer: It depends on which problem you are solving. A visiting tutor supplies supervision and presence, needs no technology at your end, and is the right answer for a child who will not engage with a screen unattended. Published market rates for in-home one-to-one run from roughly AED 180 to 500 because travel sits inside the rate. What the model cannot do in Al Ain is widen the pool of people who have taught Extended physics to examination standard, and on a narrow specialism that pool is the binding constraint. IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE.

faqs.question: Does an ADEK inspection report tell me how good my child's physics teaching is?
faqs.answer: Only indirectly. The Department of Education and Knowledge supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the Emirate of Abu Dhabi and inspects them, but a whole-school judgement aggregates every subject and every phase. A strong school can have a thin year of separate-science staffing and a mid-rated school can have an excellent Extended physics teacher. The questions that predict your child's experience are narrower: who teaches Year 11 physics, how many periods a week, which practical route the centre enters, and whether the syllabus will be finished before the mock.

faqs.question: What does 0625 physics tuition cost per hour in this market?
faqs.answer: Published figures put qualified online subject tutoring at roughly AED 150 to 300 an hour and IGCSE or A-Level specialists from about AED 200 to 450 and above, with TutorChase publishing AED 270 and Bestimate's rate table giving 200 to 450 and above. Budget online tutoring sits lower, with EdFlik listing from AED 45 to 65 and Tutopiya from AED 33 to 52. Visiting in-home rates run from about AED 180 to 500 with travel inside them. Those are other people's published numbers. Our own arrangement opens with a free trial lesson and a conversation about the weeks remaining.

faqs.question: Is Pearson International GCSE Physics easier than Cambridge 0625?
faqs.answer: Neither is easier in any way a parent can use. They are differently shaped qualifications from different boards, with their own specifications, papers and treatment of practical skills, and your child is entered for whichever one their school offers. The decision that matters is not which board to prefer but which board's material to revise from. A student working through Cambridge past papers for a Pearson entry, or the reverse, wastes evenings on content and question styles that will not appear. Confirm the specification code on the statement of entry and use that board's own published material.

al-ain/cambridge-igcse-physics-0625-tuto.closingHeading: Pick the option that matches the problem
al-ain/cambridge-igcse-physics-0625-tuto.closingBody: If your child has not been taught a topic, ask the school first and consider a group class. If they have been taught everything and the mock still came back weak, the gap is diagnosis and technique, and that is what one-to-one teaching with marked scripts is for. Send the mock script, the syllabus code from the statement of entry and the series your child is sitting, and the free trial lesson will tell you which of the six topic areas need hours and whether the practical component has been planned at all. Lessons then run one-to-one over live video in a Gulf Standard Time slot that survives an Al Ain school week.

intro.heading: Most Cambridge marks are lost in the paperwork, not the teaching
paragraphs: Cambridge International is an examination board with an administrative machine behind it, and a surprising share of the grades lost in Al Ain each year are lost inside that machine rather than inside the subject. A student entered at the wrong tier cannot reach the top grades however well they are taught. A family that works from a timetable found online rather than the one issued for their centre's zone can miss a paper. An entry deadline passing in November decides what a student sits in February. None of this is academic difficulty, and all of it is avoidable.

That is why a Cambridge IGCSE tutor in Al Ain should begin with the specification sheet. Cambridge identifies every syllabus by a four-digit code, and the code carries more information than the subject name does: which papers are sat, whether the grades are reported as A* to G or 9 to 1, whether practical science is assessed by a laboratory test or by a written alternative, and whether the subject is tiered at all. Two students at neighbouring Al Ain schools, both described as doing Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry, can be sitting different papers for differently reported grades.

Al Ain gives this a local edge. The city is part of the Emirate of Abu Dhabi, so every private school here is inspected by the Department of Education and Knowledge rather than KHDA, and the city's British-curriculum schools split between Cambridge and Pearson, sometimes running one board for sciences and another for mathematics in the same year group. The school website is frequently a year behind the actual entries. The specification sheet or the statement of entry is the authoritative document, and it is the one a parent should ask for before buying any tuition.

This page works through the administration in order: what a syllabus code tells you, the six administrative zones and the timetable risk they create, the series and their entry deadlines using Cambridge's own published key dates, how the two grading scales differ, how Cambridge and Pearson diverge on the same subject, how practical science is assessed when there is no practical examination, and the private candidate route. Then what Cambridge tuition costs in this market, with every AED figure attributed to the provider that published it.

Lessons are delivered one-to-one over live video, timed to Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE; visiting tutors are a service available only in India. On a Cambridge page that is more than a disclosure, because the material a session needs most is the student's own marked script beside the official mark scheme on a shared screen, which is easier to work with on video than across a kitchen table.

al-ain/cambridge-igcse-tutor.programmesIntro: Cambridge runs a staged pathway rather than a single qualification, and Al Ain schools use different parts of it. Knowing where your child sits in the sequence decides what the next two years should be building.

programmes.name: Cambridge IGCSE
programmes.description: Subject-by-subject qualifications identified by four-digit codes, with most subjects assessed entirely by terminal papers. Several subjects are tiered: Core entry covers a reduced content range with a restricted grade ceiling, Extended covers the full range with access to the top grades. Sciences add a practical component assessed either by a laboratory test or by a written alternative, decided by the centre.
programmes.countryNote: In Al Ain the Cambridge cohort is concentrated in a handful of British-curriculum and Indian-curriculum schools, several of which run some subjects under Pearson. Because tiering is set per subject rather than per student, a single Al Ain candidate can hold Core entry in one subject and Extended in another, and families frequently do not know which until the statement of entry arrives.

programmes.name: Cambridge Lower Secondary Checkpoint
programmes.description: Diagnostic tests taken before the IGCSE years, available in March, May and October sittings. They are not a qualification and carry no grade a university sees. Their value is diagnostic: they produce subject-level feedback that shows where a student stands against the Cambridge curriculum framework before the tier decision has to be made.
programmes.countryNote: Where an Al Ain school runs Checkpoint, the results are the single best piece of evidence available for the Core or Extended conversation a year later. Where the school does not, the tier decision rests on internal assessment alone, which is why families at those schools often ask for a diagnostic session instead before Year 10 begins.

programmes.name: Cambridge International AS and A Level
programmes.description: The usual continuation for Cambridge IGCSE students at Al Ain schools that do not run the Diploma. Advanced Subsidiary can be taken as a qualification in its own right or as the first half of the full Advanced Level. The step from Extended IGCSE in the same subject is steeper than most Year 11 students expect, particularly in mathematics and the sciences.
programmes.countryNote: The Ministry of Education's British-track equivalency route is written around Advanced and Advanced Subsidiary Levels, which gives this pathway a practical attraction for Al Ain families intending to apply to UAE institutions. Confirm the current requirements on the Ministry's own site rather than relying on a summary.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: The other post-sixteen destination for Cambridge IGCSE students, offered by a small number of Al Ain campuses. Six subjects plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and Creativity, Activity, Service, with internal assessment carrying roughly twenty to thirty per cent of most subject grades. The move from terminal-paper assessment to coursework-weighted assessment is the real adjustment.
programmes.countryNote: An Extended IGCSE student moving into the Diploma in Al Ain usually needs the most support on the first internal assessment, because nothing in the Cambridge route required a designed investigation reported against criteria. Mathematics is the other pressure point, since Extended 0580 contains no calculus.

al-ain/cambridge-igcse-tutor.subjectsIntro: Below are the Cambridge IGCSE subjects Al Ain families most often ask about, with the code families usually meet and the component that actually decides the grade. Always check the exact code on your child's own specification sheet.

subjects.name: Mathematics
subjects.description: Two papers per tier, no coursework, calculator permitted on one. Extended marks go on method lines left unwritten and on answers rounded before the final step. The tier decision matters more here than anywhere else, because Core caps the achievable grade and a capped grade blocks several A Level and Diploma routes.

subjects.name: Additional Mathematics
subjects.description: Taken alongside 0580 Extended by students heading for A Level Mathematics or Higher Level Analysis and Approaches. It includes calculus and trigonometric identities that Extended 0580 does not, and in Al Ain it is the clearest available bridge for a student who would otherwise meet differentiation cold in Year 12.

subjects.name: International Mathematics
subjects.description: A separate syllabus with a graphical-calculator expectation and an investigation element, used by some international schools instead of 0580. A tutor who has only taught 0580 will misjudge both the calculator expectations and the question styles, which is why matching on the code rather than the subject name matters.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Theory papers plus a practical component, either a laboratory test or a written alternative depending on the centre. Marks are lost by substituting before stating which quantity is held constant, and by quoting a gradient without its unit. Electricity and waves are the Al Ain cohort's recurring weak topics.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Moles arithmetic and organic chemistry account for most of the Extended gap. The practical component rewards knowing how an experiment is designed and what would make it unreliable, which is examinable in writing even where no laboratory test is sat.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Breadth rather than depth is the difficulty, and command terms decide a large share of marks. Describe, explain and suggest carry different expectations, and a student writing an explanation for a describe question loses time without gaining credit.

subjects.name: Co-ordinated and Combined Sciences
subjects.description: Routes that award one or two grades across all three sciences rather than three separate grades. Several Al Ain schools use them for students taking a broader subject spread. The content per discipline is reduced, which changes what A Level and Diploma entry a student can realistically request afterwards.

subjects.name: English First Language
subjects.description: Directed writing and composition against a stated audience and purpose, plus reading response. Marks go on failing to adopt the specified form and register rather than on technical accuracy, which is why strong writers can sit a band below where their parents expect.

subjects.name: English as a Second Language
subjects.description: Different syllabus codes for routes with and without a separately assessed speaking component. The distinction matters for Ministry of Education equivalency counting and for school entry requirements, so the code should be checked rather than assumed from the subject title.

subjects.name: Business Studies and Economics
subjects.description: Both reward applying a named concept to the stimulus rather than defining it. In Economics, diagram accuracy decides more marks than prose quality, and a diagram drawn without labelled axes and a shifted curve identified cannot earn the analysis marks regardless of the writing around it.

subjects.name: Computer Science
subjects.description: Pseudocode conventions are the board's own, and students lose marks writing valid Python where the mark scheme expects Cambridge pseudocode. Trace tables and logic gates are the most reliably examinable and most reliably under-practised parts of the syllabus.

subjects.name: Arabic
subjects.description: Mandatory alongside the international curriculum for the groups the regulator specifies, and heavily requested in Al Ain. The first-language and foreign-language syllabuses are different examinations with different expectations, and placement in the wrong one is a recurring local problem.

al-ain/cambridge-igcse-tutor.regionsIntro: Where a household sits in Al Ain changes which schools are realistic and when a weekday session can start. For Year 10 and 11 students the usable slot is earlier than for sixth formers.

regions.name: Al Jimi
regions.note: Central and close to several Cambridge-entering schools, with short school runs. A half past four start works here, which leaves room for a second session for a sibling.

regions.name: Al Mutaredh
regions.note: Older central district by the Al Ain Oasis, within reach of the city's longest-established British-curriculum campuses. Mixed-board households are common, with Cambridge sciences and Pearson mathematics in one family.

regions.name: Falaj Hazza
regions.note: South-west, with overlapping catchments and families deciding between campuses on different boards. The question of which board a school actually entered is live here every admissions season.

regions.name: Asharej
regions.note: East of the centre near United Arab Emirates University. Households include academic staff who ask early about how Cambridge grades map onto local university entry requirements.

regions.name: Zakher
regions.note: Southern villa belt with long runs into the centre, so the school run lands late. A fixed online slot at seven works where a visiting arrangement would fail in the first fortnight.

regions.name: Al Muwaiji
regions.note: Western and heavily Emirati, with strong demand for Arabic first language alongside the Cambridge subjects. Placement between the first-language and foreign-language syllabuses is the frequent issue.

regions.note: Near the hospital campus, where shift rotas shape availability. Families here often prefer a weekend slot to a weekday one, which video delivery makes straightforward.

schoolClusters.note: Schools whose middle years run an IB framework or a mixed model, with some cohorts still sitting international GCSE papers. al-ain/cambridge-igcse-tutor.modesIntro: Cambridge support divides naturally by where the student is in the two-year cycle. All three formats below are delivered one-to-one over live video, timed to Gulf Standard Time.

modes.title: Tier-decision diagnostic, one to three sessions
modes.description: A short block before or early in Year 10, aimed entirely at the Core or Extended question in one or two subjects. The tutor works through Extended-standard questions with the student, identifies whether the gap is content, confidence or pace, and produces a written view the family can take to the school. The tier is set by the centre, but a parent arguing for Extended needs evidence rather than a preference.
bullets: Extended-standard questions worked under observation, not discussed
A written summary of what the student can and cannot yet do
Timed to land before the school's internal tiering decision

modes.title: Weekly syllabus support through Years 10 and 11
modes.description: A fixed slot in one subject, worked against the named syllabus code rather than a generic subject plan, running alongside the school's scheme of work. The balance shifts from content to timed questions from the start of the final two terms, and from the mock window onwards the work is almost entirely past papers marked against official mark schemes.
bullets: Matched to the exact code, including the practical component the centre entered
A written note after each session listing what was covered and set
Reviewed after each school assessment, not on a monthly cycle

modes.title: Pre-series intensive, eight to ten weeks
modes.description: A concentrated block before a series, built on timed papers worked in the order the student will sit them. The focus is command terms, mark tariffs and timing: how long a four-mark question deserves, which verb changes the required answer, and where a student is spending twelve minutes on six marks. Most late grade movement comes from this rather than from new content.
bullets: Papers worked to time and marked against official mark schemes
A per-paper target rather than one target grade
Built around the zone timetable the centre actually sits

sections.heading: What a four-digit syllabus code tells you that the subject name does not
paragraphs: Cambridge identifies each syllabus with a four-digit code, and the code is the only reliable description of what a student is sitting. It fixes the number and type of papers, whether the subject is tiered, how practical work is assessed and which grading scale is reported. Two Al Ain students both described as taking Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics may be sitting 0580 or 0607, which differ in calculator expectation, question style and whether an investigation forms part of the assessment.

Cambridge also publishes paired syllabuses for several subjects: one version reported on the A* to G scale and one on the 9 to 1 scale, each with its own code. The content is closely aligned, the reporting is not, and a school chooses which to enter. A parent who reads a grade boundary table or a past paper for the wrong member of the pair is working from the wrong document. The practical rule is that the code on the specification sheet or the statement of entry is authoritative, and anything inferred from a subject name is a guess.

There is a further wrinkle that affects Al Ain families with children at different schools. Tiering is set per subject, not per student, and it is a centre decision. A single candidate can be entered for Core in one subject and Extended in another, and the first time many families see the complete picture is when the statement of entry arrives, by which point changing a tier is difficult and sometimes impossible. Asking the school in writing, in the first term of Year 10, which tier is intended in each subject is a ten-minute task that prevents a year of misdirected work.

sections.heading: Six administrative zones, and the timetable that is actually yours
paragraphs: Cambridge states that every centre is allocated to one of six administrative zones, and that it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for your zone. It also states that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an examination after using the wrong zone timetable. That second sentence is the reason this belongs on a tutoring page rather than being left to the school: the consequence of the error falls entirely on the candidate.

The practical risk in Al Ain is specific and recurring. A parent searching online for a Cambridge timetable finds a timetable, often a British one, and plans around it. Travel is booked, a grandparent's visit is arranged, a family trip is scheduled in what looks like a gap. The zone timetable the centre actually sits puts a paper in that gap. Because the examination windows across zones can differ by days, the error is subtle enough to survive a casual check.

The correct procedure is unglamorous. Ask the school's examinations officer which zone the centre sits in and for the zone-specific timetable as issued, and work from that single document for the whole series. Then check the statement of entry against it, paper by paper, because the statement of entry is also where a wrong tier or a missing component shows up while there is still time to raise it.

For tutoring this has one more consequence. A pre-series intensive should be built around the order in which the student will actually sit the papers in their zone, not the order Cambridge lists them in the syllabus. A student sitting two science papers on consecutive days needs a different final fortnight from one with a week between them, and that information lives in the zone timetable and nowhere else.
bullets: Ask the examinations officer which zone the centre sits in, and get that timetable
Check the statement of entry against it paper by paper, in good time
Plan the final fortnight around the real paper order, not the syllabus order
Never plan travel from a timetable found by a web search

sections.heading: The series, and the deadlines that sit months before the papers
paragraphs: Cambridge runs IGCSE, O Level and International A Level examinations in a June series and a November series, with Primary and Lower Secondary Checkpoint tests in March, May and October. Cambridge also publishes key dates for a March series, and that series is the clearest published illustration of how far ahead the administration sits relative to the examinations themselves.

For the Cambridge March 2027 series, the published key dates are: examination period 3 February to 4 March 2027, final entries due 27 November 2026, forecast grades due 27 February 2027, results on Cambridge Direct on 13 May, and certificates in late June. Read backwards, that sequence says something important to any Al Ain parent. The decision about which subjects a student sits, and at which tier, is effectively locked more than two months before the first paper. An argument for moving a student from Core to Extended, made in January, is usually too late to act on.

Forecast grades deserve a note of their own, because families frequently confuse them with predicted grades for university applications. A forecast grade is submitted by the centre to the board as part of administering the series. It is the school's professional judgement of the grade the candidate is expected to achieve, and it sits in the results process rather than in the admissions process. It is not something a tutor can influence directly, and a tutor who offers to is misunderstanding the mechanism.

sections.heading: Nine to one, or A star to G: which scale is your child's grade on?
paragraphs: Cambridge reports IGCSE results on two scales. The long-established scale runs from A* down to G, and the newer numeric scale runs from 9 down to 1, with 9 as the highest. Each is attached to its own syllabus code, so the scale is a consequence of what the centre entered rather than something decided at results time. A parent cannot tell which scale applies from the subject name, and the two are not interchangeable when reading boundaries or comparing with an older sibling's results.

The grades are designed to be broadly comparable rather than identical, and the mapping is not one-to-one at every point: the numeric scale subdivides the top of the old scale more finely, which is the whole reason it exists. Treating a 7 as equivalent to an A, or a 9 as simply an A*, loses the distinction the scale was built to make. For a UAE family comparing an older child's A* against a younger child's 8, that distinction matters when reading a school's entry requirements.

Where this bites practically is in school and university entry requirements, which may be written in either scale or in both. An Al Ain school's sixth-form entry requirement expressed as a grade 6 is not the same as one expressed as a B, and families applying across institutions can meet both forms on the same day. The Ministry of Education's equivalency rule for the British track is expressed in the older terms, specifying five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at no less than grade E or grade 3, which is itself an example of a requirement written to cover both scales.

The useful habit is to record, for each subject, the code and the scale, and to carry that single line into every conversation about entry requirements. It takes one sheet of paper and removes a whole category of confusion that otherwise surfaces at the worst moment.
bullets: The scale follows the syllabus code the centre entered, not the subject
Nine to one subdivides the top of the old scale; it is not a rename
Entry requirements may be written in either scale, sometimes both

sections.heading: The same subject under Cambridge and under Pearson
paragraphs: Al Ain's British-curriculum schools split between Cambridge International and Pearson Edexcel, and some run both for different subjects in the same year group. Universities treat the two as equivalent qualifications. Students do not experience them as equivalent, because the papers, the tiering, the practical arrangements and the assessment rhythm differ, and a tutor fluent in one board's mark scheme will misread the other's.

The clearest structural difference is in how the series work. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE examinations are available in May or June and in November each year, and Pearson publishes provisional timetables ahead of each series, including for International GCSE November 2027, so the live official timetable is always the document to use. For the November 2026 series the final timetable runs from late October to 19 November 2026. Pearson results for June 2026 went to centres on 19 August 2026 and to students on 20 August 2026, and November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. Those published dates give a family a concrete sense of the gap between a paper and a result, which is longer than most expect.

Beyond administration, the differences that reach the student are in question style and in practical science. Boards structure extended-response questions differently and reward different levels of explicit working, and the practical component may be a laboratory test or a written alternative depending on both the board and the centre's choice. A student moving school mid-course between boards is therefore making a genuine transition, not a formality, and it is worth a short block of support rather than being treated as a change of textbook.

sections.heading: Practical science when the tuition happens on a screen
paragraphs: This is the honest question every science parent asks, and it deserves a direct answer rather than reassurance. Cambridge assesses practical skills in IGCSE sciences either through a laboratory test or through a written alternative, and the centre decides which. In both cases the assessment is of practical reasoning rather than of manual technique: identifying the variable to control, spotting what would make a result unreliable, reading a scale correctly, choosing an appropriate apparatus, explaining why a repeat matters.

All of that is examinable in writing and teachable on a shared screen. A tutor can work through a method and ask what is wrong with it, present a results table with an anomaly and ask what to do about it, or give a graph with poorly chosen axes and ask why the gradient is unreliable. That is precisely the cognitive work the practical component tests. What a tutor cannot do remotely is supervise the physical handling of apparatus, and nobody should claim otherwise.

The division of labour is therefore clear. The school laboratory is where the hands-on work happens, under the school's own supervision and safety arrangements, and where a laboratory test is taken if the centre has entered one. Tuition covers the reasoning, the recording conventions, the uncertainty treatment and the question technique. In Al Ain, where several schools enter the written alternative rather than the laboratory test, this division means the component is almost entirely accessible to online support.

No Cambridge past papers, mark schemes, syllabus documents or grade-boundary tables are supplied as downloads here or in a session. They are Cambridge's copyright and the official site is where they belong; a session works from them by reference and by link rather than by distribution.
bullets: The centre chooses between a laboratory test and the written alternative
Practical reasoning, not manual technique, is what the component tests

sections.heading: The private candidate route from Al Ain
paragraphs: Sometimes a subject a student needs is not entered by their school, or a student is studying outside a school altogether, or a resit is wanted in a series the school is not entering. In those cases the route is to sit as a private candidate at a registered Cambridge examination centre, which is a different arrangement from being entered by one's own school and comes with its own conditions.

Three things determine whether it is feasible. First, a centre must be willing to accept private candidates, which not all do, and the acceptance usually has to be arranged well before the entry deadline. Second, not every syllabus is available to private candidates, because some have components that require a centre to assess coursework or speaking. Third, the fees are the candidate's own and are set by the centre rather than by the board, so they vary and must be asked for directly.

For an Al Ain family this is a logistical question before it is an academic one, since the nearest centre accepting private candidates may be in Abu Dhabi rather than in the city. That turns each paper into a journey on a date fixed by the zone timetable. Planning that around a multi-paper series is the part families underestimate, and it is worth mapping before committing to the route rather than after.

Where tuition fits is straightforward: a private candidate has no class, no school mock and no teacher submitting forecast grades, so the structure that a cohort provides has to be built deliberately. That means a schedule with fixed checkpoints, full papers sat to time at the right intervals, and an honest external view of where the student actually stands. It is demanding, and it works for the right student with the right subject.
bullets: Not every centre accepts private candidates; arrange it early
Some syllabuses are unavailable privately because of their components
Entry fees are set by the centre, not the board, so ask directly
Without a cohort, the structure has to be built deliberately

sections.heading: What Cambridge tuition costs in this market, and the limits on this page
paragraphs: Published UAE tutoring rates range widely and most pages competing for this search print no AED figure. The bands below are market rates taken from providers' own published pricing and from Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 rate table. They describe the market rather than IB Gram's price list, and they are here so that an Al Ain quote can be measured against something checkable. Budget online tutoring from university students is advertised from roughly AED 45 to 150 an hour, with EdFlik from AED 45 to 65 and Tutopiya from roughly AED 33 to 52. A qualified subject tutor working online sits at AED 150 to 300, where Unitors publishes IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200. In-home one-to-one with travel runs roughly AED 180 to 500, with Bestimate at 180 to 350 and independent home tutors at 200 to 500. IGCSE and A Level specialists run AED 200 to 450 and above, with TutorChase at AED 270, and premium named tutoring reaches AED 650, as BartyED publishes.

Bestimate's monthly estimates for weekly one-hour sessions are AED 240 to 600 at the budget end, AED 600 to 1,200 mid-market and AED 1,000 to 2,000 and above for specialist examination-year support. Monthly packages seen in the market include AED 799 for eight online sessions. For a Cambridge candidate the sensible shape is usually a steady weekly hour through Year 10 and the first part of Year 11, then a heavier pre-series block. Paying specialist examination-year rates from the first week of Year 10 is a common overspend, and the exception worth making is the tier-decision diagnostic, where a small number of hours early can change the grade ceiling for two years.

The limits on this page are worth stating plainly. IB Gram holds no approval, accreditation, licence or partnership from Cambridge International, Pearson, ADEK, KHDA, the Ministry of Education or the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation, and there is no IB Gram office, centre or branch anywhere in the UAE. No grade is promised by anyone here and no statistic appears without a named source. Lessons are delivered one-to-one over live video, timed to Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE; visiting tutors are a service available only in India. Where no UAE-based specialist is free for a syllabus, the match comes from the wider tutor pool at Gulf Standard Time and that is disclosed before any lesson is booked.

One further point applies to any tutor an Al Ain family hires, from us or anywhere. Private tutoring in the UAE is regulated by permit. The private tutor work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is granted free of charge for two years, and covers teachers registered in government or private schools, government and private sector employees, unemployed individuals, school students aged 15 to 18 and university students. The Ministry's service is Issuance of a New Work Permit - Private Tutor Licensing, listing no fees and a two-working-day completion time, applied for through its smart app, website and e-services system. Anyone tutoring without a permit is subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws; no fine schedule is published, so no amount is quoted here.

process.title: Send the specification sheet or statement of entry
process.description: Not the subject list from the school website. The specification sheet or statement of entry carries the four-digit codes, the tiers and the components actually entered, and it is the only document that reliably describes what your child is sitting. Everything else in the process follows from it.

process.title: Get the zone timetable from the examinations officer
process.description: Cambridge allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones and warns that the correct zone timetable must be used. Ask which zone the centre sits in and work from the issued timetable for the whole series, then check it against the statement of entry paper by paper.

process.title: Settle the tier question with evidence
process.description: If Core or Extended is in doubt, a short diagnostic produces a written view of what the student can currently do at Extended standard. The tier is the centre's decision, but a case made with evidence in the first term of Year 10 lands very differently from a preference raised in January.

process.title: Meet the matched tutor for a trial lesson at no charge
process.description: One introductory session once a tutor is matched to the exact syllabus code, with nothing charged and no card required to book. Watch whether the tutor asks for the code and the practical component before teaching, which is the clearest signal that the match is real rather than nominal.

process.title: Review after each school assessment
process.description: Mock results and marked school papers are the review points, because they show component marks rather than impressions. Diagnose by component and by question type, and change the plan when the evidence says so rather than persisting with a diagnosis that the last paper contradicted.

whyPoints.title: The code comes before the teaching
whyPoints.description: Matching a tutor to 0580 Extended or 0607 or 0606 is not pedantry. The papers, tiering, calculator expectations and mark schemes differ, and a tutor working from the wrong one teaches confidently in the wrong direction.

whyPoints.title: Administration treated as part of the grade
whyPoints.description: Zone timetables, entry deadlines and tier decisions decide outcomes before any teaching happens. Most pages competing for this search mention none of them, and most of the avoidable grade losses in Al Ain each year sit here.

whyPoints.title: Dates taken from the board, not aggregated
whyPoints.description: The Cambridge and Pearson dates on this page come from each board's own published key dates and timetable pages, with the series named. No IB session date appears anywhere here, because the IB's own site is the only reliable source for those.

whyPoints.title: Al Ain's regulator, correctly identified
whyPoints.description: Al Ain private schools are inspected by ADEK, not KHDA. Almost all online tutoring content is written about Dubai, which points a local parent at the wrong authority and the wrong inspection framework.

whyPoints.title: Rates with sources attached
whyPoints.description: Every AED band here is attributed to the provider or rate table that published it and kept separate from anything IB Gram charges. Three of the six pages competing in this market publish no price at all.

whyPoints.title: Official materials referenced, not distributed
whyPoints.description: Past papers, mark schemes, syllabus documents and boundary tables stay on Cambridge's own site. Sessions work from them by link and by reference, which is both the lawful position and the only version guaranteed current.

faqs.question: What do Cambridge syllabus codes like 0580 and 0620 tell me?
faqs.answer: They identify the exact syllabus, which the subject name does not. The code fixes how many papers are sat, whether the subject is tiered into Core and Extended, how practical work is assessed and which grading scale the result is reported on. Cambridge publishes paired syllabuses for several subjects, one reported A* to G and one 9 to 1, each with its own code. Take the code from your child's specification sheet or statement of entry, and verify it on Cambridge International's own subject pages, because syllabuses are revised and codes retire.

faqs.question: Which Cambridge administrative zone is Al Ain in, and why does it matter?
faqs.answer: The zone belongs to the centre rather than to the city, so ask your school's examinations officer which zone it sits in. It matters because Cambridge allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones, states that using the correct zone timetable is essential, and says it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an examination after using the wrong one. Examination windows across zones differ by days, which is subtle enough that a parent planning travel from a timetable found online may not notice until it is too late.

faqs.question: What is the difference between the Cambridge March, June and November series?
faqs.answer: Cambridge runs IGCSE, O Level and International A Level examinations in a June series and a November series, and publishes key dates for a March series as well. Checkpoint tests sit in March, May and October. The practical difference for a family is resit timing: a November series means a student who misses a target in the summer can retake within months rather than waiting a year. Which series your school enters is a centre decision, so ask rather than assume, and work only from the official timetable issued for that series.

faqs.question: When do Cambridge final entries close for a March series?
faqs.answer: For the March 2027 series Cambridge publishes final entries as due on 27 November 2026, with the examination period running 3 February to 4 March 2027, forecast grades due 27 February 2027, results on Cambridge Direct on 13 May and certificates in late June. The gap is the point: subject and tier decisions are effectively locked more than two months before the first paper. If you want a tier changed, the conversation belongs in the first term of Year 10, not in the new year when the entries are already submitted.

faqs.question: What is a forecast grade and who submits it to Cambridge?
faqs.answer: A forecast grade is the centre's professional judgement of the grade a candidate is expected to achieve, submitted by the school to Cambridge as part of administering a series. For the March 2027 series Cambridge publishes the forecast grades deadline as 27 February 2027. It is part of the results process rather than the university admissions process, which is where predicted grades belong, and the two are often confused. No tutor can influence a forecast grade directly, and any offer to do so misunderstands how the mechanism works.

faqs.question: Is my child's Cambridge IGCSE graded 9 to 1 or A* to G?
faqs.answer: It depends on which syllabus code the centre entered, because Cambridge attaches the scale to the syllabus rather than deciding it at results time. The numeric scale subdivides the top of the older scale more finely, which is why it exists, so a 7 is not simply an A. Keep a single sheet listing each subject's code and scale, because school and university entry requirements may be written in either form. The Ministry of Education's British-track equivalency rule names grade E or grade 3 precisely to cover both.

faqs.question: How are Cambridge IGCSE science practicals assessed?
faqs.answer: Either through a laboratory test or through a written alternative, with the centre choosing which and choosing separately per subject. In both cases what is examined is practical reasoning rather than manual dexterity: identifying controlled variables, spotting what makes a result unreliable, reading scales, choosing apparatus and justifying repeats. That reasoning is teachable on a shared screen using methods, results tables and graphs. The hands-on work stays in the school laboratory under the school's own supervision and safety arrangements.

faqs.question: Can my child sit Cambridge IGCSE as a private candidate in Al Ain?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, with three conditions. A registered Cambridge centre must be willing to accept private candidates, and not all do, so the arrangement has to be made well before the entry deadline. Not every syllabus is available privately, because some components require centre assessment. And entry fees are set by the centre rather than the board, so ask the centre directly. For Al Ain families the nearest accepting centre may be in Abu Dhabi, which turns each paper into a journey on a date fixed by the zone timetable.

faqs.question: Is Cambridge IGCSE or Pearson Edexcel International GCSE better for a UAE student?
faqs.answer: Universities treat them as equivalent, so the better board is whichever your child's centre has entered. What differs is the experience: series timing, question styles, tiering arrangements and how practical science is assessed. Pearson runs May or June and November series and publishes provisional then final timetables; Cambridge runs June and November with published key dates for a March series and allocates centres to administrative zones. A student changing school mid-course between boards is making a real transition and usually benefits from a short block of support.

faqs.question: Which Cambridge IGCSE subjects do Al Ain students most often resit?
faqs.answer: Mathematics first, then the individual sciences, with English First Language appearing more often than families expect. Mathematics resits are frequently a tier issue rather than a teaching issue: a student capped by Core entry who needed Extended for a sixth-form or Diploma route. The November series makes a resit possible within months rather than a year, which is worth knowing before results day so the decision can be made quickly. Ask the school which subjects it will enter in November before assuming the option exists.

faqs.question: How many Cambridge IGCSE subjects does the Ministry of Education count?
faqs.answer: Five. As reported when the UAE clarified its equivalency requirements, a student must pass five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates with a grade of no less than E or grade 3, and Arabic and Islamic education are not included among those five. The British track also requires proof of one accredited Advanced Level subject at no less than E, or two Advanced Subsidiary subjects at the same grade. One ranking competitor tells UAE families six subjects are required; the sourced figure is five. Confirm the current rules on the Ministry's own site.

faqs.question: What is Cambridge Lower Secondary Checkpoint and does it matter?
faqs.answer: Checkpoint is a set of diagnostic tests taken in the years before IGCSE, available in March, May and October sittings. It is not a qualification and no university sees it. Its value is that it produces subject-level evidence of where a student stands against the Cambridge framework before the Core or Extended decision has to be made, which is the single most consequential decision of the IGCSE years. Where an Al Ain school does not run it, families often ask for a diagnostic session instead before Year 10 starts.

faqs.question: Can one tutor cover Cambridge IGCSE Maths 0580 and Additional Maths 0606?
faqs.answer: Often yes, and it is one of the more sensible pairings to keep with a single tutor, because 0606 builds directly on Extended 0580 and introduces calculus and trigonometric identities that 0580 does not contain. Ask when the tutor last taught 0606 specifically, since the calculus content and question style differ enough that general mathematics teaching does not automatically cover it. For a student heading towards A Level Mathematics or Higher Level Analysis and Approaches, 0606 is the most useful bridge available in Al Ain.

faqs.question: How long before a Cambridge paper should tutoring start?
faqs.answer: Earlier than most families start, and for a different reason than they expect. The highest-value early work is not content but the tier decision, because Core entry caps the achievable grade and the entry is effectively locked months before the paper. After that, a steady weekly hour through Year 10 and the first part of Year 11 costs less and achieves more than a heavy final block alone. A pre-series intensive of eight to ten weeks on timed papers is where most late grade movement comes from, so plan both.

faqs.question: What does a Cambridge IGCSE tutor charge in Al Ain?
faqs.answer: Judge any quote against the published market. Unitors publishes IGCSE tutoring from AED 150 an hour; TutorChase publishes AED 270; Bestimate's rate table puts specialists at AED 200 to 450 and above and budget online tutoring at the lower end, with EdFlik advertising from AED 45 to 65. Bestimate's monthly estimate for a weekly one-hour session is AED 600 to 1,200 mid-market. IB Gram publishes no rate card here; the next step is a trial lesson at no charge once a tutor is matched to the syllabus code, then a quote against the actual subject and tier.

al-ain/cambridge-igcse-tutor.closingBody: Find the document that lists your child's four-digit syllabus codes, the tier entered in each subject and the practical components, then ask the examinations officer which administrative zone the centre sits in and get that timetable. Those two pieces of paper answer more questions than any amount of general advice, and they are what any competent Cambridge tutor will ask for first. Send them to us with one marked school paper and we will match a tutor to the code rather than to the subject name. Lessons are one-to-one over live video at Gulf Standard Time; home visits are an India-only service and are not offered anywhere in the UAE.

al-ain/falaj-hazza.heroSubtitle: IB and IGCSE tutors in Falaj Hazza are frequently hired to repair a decision rather than to teach a topic. A tier entry at fourteen, a board at fifteen, a mathematics route at sixteen and a level on six subjects at once each cap what a student can be awarded before a paper is sat. This page sets out who makes each decision, when it can still be changed, and what one-to-one online support can and cannot do about it afterwards.

al-ain/falaj-hazza.tutorsIntro: The tutors below are matched to a specific decision as well as a subject: securing algebra before a tier entry, converting between two boards' paper structures, and building the readiness that makes a Higher Level choice realistic rather than aspirational.

intro.heading: Four decisions, each one capping a grade before a paper is sat
paragraphs: Falaj Hazza sits west of central Al Ain, closer to the school cluster than the southern districts and denser than most of the city, with a mixture of family villas and low apartment blocks along its main streets. Journeys into school are short by Al Ain standards, which means households here have more usable evening hours than families further out. What they ask about, as a result, is rarely scheduling. It is choices.

Four of those choices matter more than anything a tutor will ever teach. At around fourteen a school decides, or a family accepts, whether a child is entered for Core or Extended tier in several IGCSE subjects, and that entry caps the grade available. At fifteen the board is fixed, which decides the paper architecture and the formula sheet. At sixteen a mathematics route is chosen that some university courses will read as a prerequisite. And at sixteen again, six subjects are assigned a level in a single afternoon of form-filling.

None of those four decisions is reversible on a comfortable timescale, and none of them is usually explained to a family in terms of what it closes. A parent is told their child has been placed in the Core group and hears a reassurance about appropriate challenge. What has actually happened is that the maximum achievable grade has been reduced, and if that was the right call the family deserves to know it was a call. If it was a default applied to a set rather than to a student, it deserves to be questioned.

This is why enquiries from this district often begin with a question that sounds administrative. Which paper is my daughter sitting? Why does my son's past paper look different from his cousin's? Can the school change the entry now? Those are the right questions, asked slightly too late, and the tutoring that follows is usually either closing a gap fast enough to justify a tier change or making the best of a ceiling that cannot now be raised.

What follows sets each decision out with the person who makes it, the point at which it hardens, and what a parent can reasonably ask for before then. It also covers the honest version of the repair work: what can be fixed in a term, what takes a year, and what cannot be fixed at all once an entry has closed. There is no benefit in pretending otherwise, because a family planning around a false hope spends money badly.

Delivery is one-to-one over live video. IB Gram does not sell home visits anywhere in the UAE and nobody will be sent to a Falaj Hazza address; that is an India-only service. Where this page quotes a market rate or an awarding-body date it names the source, and where a figure could not be verified it is left out, which is why no IB examination dates appear anywhere on this site.
