al-ain/ib-dp-math-aa-sl-tutor.programmesIntro: Four of the IB routes below are the ones an Al Ain Diploma family is choosing between in the first weeks of DP1. We teach all four, which is why we are willing to say when a student is in the wrong one rather than selling hours against it.

programmes.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches SL
programmes.description: The algebra-and-calculus route taken at Standard Level: 150 guided hours, two papers of 1 hour 30 minutes at 40 per cent each, and a 20 per cent exploration. Content covers sequences and series, the binomial theorem, logarithms and exponentials, trigonometric identities and equations, differentiation including the chain, product and quotient rules, and integration to the area under a curve.
programmes.countryNote: In Al Ain this is the commonest Standard Level maths class, partly because it is often the only one timetabled. Students arriving from a Cambridge IGCSE Extended background usually cope with the functions work and struggle with the pace of the calculus block in the second half of DP1, which lands in the same term as the first exploration deadlines at most Al Ain schools.

programmes.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation SL
programmes.description: The modelling-and-statistics route at the same level and the same 150 hours. A graphic display calculator is required in both papers. Content shifts towards regression, the chi-squared test for independence, financial mathematics, approximation and percentage error, Voronoi diagrams and three-dimensional solids, with a much lighter calculus load that stops short of integration by substitution.
programmes.countryNote: Where an Al Ain school runs both Standard Level routes, this is the one students transfer into rather than out of. It suits a student heading for business, psychology, design, media or most social sciences, and it is the route that rewards a student who is better at interpreting a data set than at manipulating an expression on paper.

programmes.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches HL
programmes.description: The Higher Level version of the same course, built on 240 guided hours and assessed across three papers plus the exploration. It adds proof by induction, complex numbers, three-dimensional vectors, differential equations and a one-hour Paper 3 of extended problem solving that is worth a fifth of the grade on its own.
programmes.countryNote: Few Al Ain cohorts are large enough to timetable Analysis and Approaches at both levels in the same block, so the step up is usually a conversation with the coordinator rather than a simple class change. Students who want the Higher Level route for an engineering application are better off raising it in DP1 than discovering the constraint in DP2.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme, years 4 and 5
programmes.description: The two years immediately before the Diploma, where extended mathematics in MYP 5 is the usual preparation for Analysis and Approaches. Assessment runs on four criteria: knowing and understanding, investigating patterns, communicating, and applying mathematics in real-life contexts, which is a very different habit from a timed written paper.
programmes.countryNote: The MYP-to-Diploma gap is the most predictable problem we see in Al Ain, because MYP assessment rewards process and explanation while Analysis and Approaches Paper 1 rewards fast, accurate, unassisted manipulation. A student who has never sat a paper without a calculator arrives in DP1 with no idea that this is a separate skill.

al-ain/ib-dp-math-aa-sl-tutor.subjectsIntro: A tutor is matched to a topic, not to the subject label. These are the blocks inside Analysis and Approaches SL that Al Ain students actually ask for, together with the two paper techniques and the exploration, which behave like separate subjects of their own.

subjects.name: Number and algebra
subjects.description: Sequences and series, the binomial theorem for positive integer exponents, index and logarithm laws, scientific notation and approximation. This is the block Paper 1 punishes hardest, because every rule here has to be applied from memory and the arithmetic has to be exact rather than close.

subjects.name: Functions
subjects.description: Domain and range, composite and inverse functions, quadratic, rational, exponential and logarithmic models, and transformations of graphs. Marks are lost on order of operations rather than concept: composing in the wrong direction, or applying a stretch after a translation when the algebra demands the opposite.

subjects.name: Geometry and trigonometry
subjects.description: Three-dimensional solids, the sine and cosine rules, radian measure, arcs and sectors, the unit circle, trigonometric identities and equations. Radians are the recurring trap: a student who sets a calculator in degrees for Paper 2 loses a chain of answers from one toggle.

subjects.name: Statistics and probability
subjects.description: Sampling and bias, measures of central tendency and dispersion, correlation and the regression line, conditional probability, the binomial distribution and the normal distribution. Paper 2 expects a calculator route to these; Paper 1 expects the tree diagram and the definition.

subjects.name: Calculus
subjects.description: Limits and the derivative from first principles, the chain, product and quotient rules, tangents and normals, optimisation, kinematics, and integration as far as definite integrals and the area under a curve. The last six weeks of DP1 usually decide whether this block is secure.

subjects.name: Paper 1 technique
subjects.description: Working without a calculator is a trainable skill: exact values from the unit circle, surd and index manipulation, factorising on sight, and keeping a fraction as a fraction rather than converting to a decimal that cannot be recovered. Most of the gain available to a Standard Level student sits here.

subjects.name: Paper 2 technique
subjects.description: Knowing which calculator function answers the question is half the paper: solving numerically, finding intersections, running a regression, using inverse normal, and then writing enough method that a correct screen value earns the marks attached to it rather than one answer mark.

subjects.name: The mathematical exploration
subjects.levels: 20 per cent of the final grade
subjects.description: A 12 to 20 page piece of independent work marked out of 20 across presentation, mathematical communication, personal engagement, reflection and use of mathematics. The commonest failure at Standard Level is a topic that forces maths above or below the course, not weak writing.

subjects.name: Algebra repair from IGCSE or MYP
subjects.description: Expanding and factorising, completing the square, rearranging formulae, index and surd laws, and sign handling in algebraic fractions. None of this is on the Diploma syllabus, and all of it is assumed by it, which is why a diagnostic session usually starts here rather than with DP content.

subjects.name: Mock and final-term paper work
subjects.description: Timed sections under real conditions, marked against the published mark scheme wording rather than a tick for the right answer. The aim is a student who knows their own reliable mark on each section and where the next three marks are, which is a different exercise from revision.

sections.heading: What an Al Ain family is really asking when they search for AA SL help
paragraphs: An IB DP Math AA SL tutor in Al Ain is being asked to answer one question before any teaching happens: is this student in the right course and underperforming, or in the wrong course and coping? The two look identical on a school report and need opposite responses. The first is a teaching problem that responds to weekly work on unassisted algebra. The second is a timetabling problem that needs a conversation with the Diploma coordinator in DP1, while a change is still practical.

The reason this matters more in Al Ain than in Dubai is cohort size. A Diploma class of fifteen does not support two Standard Level maths routes in the same option block, so a student may be sitting Analysis and Approaches because it was the class that ran. In a larger school both Standard Level routes sit side by side and the student picks. Neither situation is anyone's fault, but only one of them can be fixed by buying hours, and a family deserves to know which one they are in before they commit a year of Sunday evenings.

The practical test is cheap. Take a marked Paper 1, sit with the student for forty minutes, and watch where the pen stops. A student with an arithmetic debt starts every question, sets up the right method and then loses the thread in the manipulation. A student in the wrong course reads the question and does not start, because the first step is an algebraic move they were never fluent in. The first student needs drilling. The second needs either a route change or a genuine rebuild of pre-Diploma algebra, which takes a term and should be described honestly as such.

Everything below assumes the answer has been established. The sections run from the two papers, through the comparison with Applications and Interpretation at the same level, into the five topics and the exploration, and finish with coverage, honesty boundaries and scheduling. A parent who reads only the tables will still finish with the information needed to ask their coordinator a sharper question than they could before.

sections.heading: Paper 1 arrives without a calculator, and that is the whole difficulty
paragraphs: Analysis and Approaches at Standard Level is assessed through two written papers and one piece of coursework. Both papers run 1 hour 30 minutes, both carry 80 marks, and each is worth 40 per cent of the final grade. The exploration carries the remaining 20 per cent. The formula booklet is supplied in both papers. The difference that decides most Standard Level grades is that no technology at all is permitted in Paper 1, while a graphic display calculator is required throughout Paper 2.

That single rule changes what is being examined. In Paper 2 a student who understands the shape of a problem can often reach the answer through the calculator: solve numerically, find the intersection, run the regression, read the inverse normal value. In Paper 1 the same understanding earns nothing unless the algebra and the arithmetic carry it. Exact values from the unit circle, surd manipulation, index and logarithm laws, factorising on sight and keeping fractions as fractions all have to be available at speed, from memory, under time pressure.

This is why the diagnostic conversation above matters so much. A student with a strong Paper 2 and a weak Paper 1 does not have a conceptual problem with Diploma mathematics; they have an unfinished IGCSE or MYP algebra habit that a calculator has concealed for three years. That is a fixable, trainable deficit, and it responds to short, frequent, unassisted practice rather than to more content teaching. Ten minutes of no-calculator work in every session for six months moves more marks than two extra topics covered.

The other side of the same coin is a student who has been told to practise without a calculator and now distrusts the device entirely. Paper 2 rewards knowing which function answers the question and writing enough method that a correct screen value attracts the method marks attached to it. Both skills need building, and they are different skills. A tutor who treats the two papers as one exam with different rules on the front cover will leave marks on both.

sections.heading: Analysis and Approaches SL against Applications and Interpretation SL
paragraphs: These two courses occupy the same timetable slot, carry the same 150 guided hours, and produce a grade on the same one-to-seven scale. They are not variations on each other. Analysis and Approaches is a course about algebraic structure, proof-adjacent reasoning and calculus. Applications and Interpretation is a course about modelling, statistics and interpretation, taught on the assumption that a calculator is always present. A student can be strong at one and genuinely weak at the other, which is why the choice deserves more than a sentence on an option form.

The content differences are concrete enough to check against a syllabus in ten minutes. Analysis and Approaches SL includes the binomial theorem, trigonometric identities and equations, logarithms and exponentials, and calculus that reaches the chain, product and quotient rules and definite integration. Applications and Interpretation SL carries none of that last group at the same depth, and instead adds the chi-squared test for independence, financial mathematics including compound interest, approximation and percentage error, Voronoi diagrams and more work on three-dimensional solids. Neither list is harder in the abstract; they reward different students.

For route signalling, published entry requirements for mathematics-facing degrees name Analysis and Approaches more often than Applications and Interpretation, particularly for engineering, physics, mathematics and some economics programmes. That pattern is real but it is not a rule, it changes between institutions and between years, and it has to be read on the programme's own admissions page rather than taken from any tutoring site including this one. A student aiming at business, psychology, design, architecture or most social sciences is rarely disadvantaged by the applications route.

In Al Ain the choice is frequently narrowed by what the school can staff. If both Standard Level routes run, a student who freezes in front of an expression on paper and comes alive in front of a data set should look hard at Applications and Interpretation before DP1 closes. If only one route runs, the question becomes whether the student can be brought up to the demands of the course that exists, and that is a judgement a specialist should make from a script rather than from a conversation.

sections.heading: The algebra Standard Level assumes and IGCSE quietly let slide
paragraphs: Nothing in the paragraphs below appears on the Diploma syllabus. All of it is assumed by it. A Cambridge or Pearson IGCSE candidate can reach a strong grade while leaning on a calculator for arithmetic, accepting partial credit on algebraic fractions, and avoiding the questions that need completing the square. Analysis and Approaches SL Paper 1 removes every one of those shelters at once, in the first mock of DP1, which is usually where an Al Ain family first realises something is wrong.

The list is short and specific. Expanding and factorising without hesitation. Index and surd laws in both directions. Completing the square as a method rather than a formula. Rearranging a formula where the subject appears twice. Sign handling in algebraic fractions. Solving simultaneous equations where one is non-linear. Reading a negative exponent correctly. None of these takes long to teach. What takes time is making them automatic, because Paper 1 does not give a student the thinking room to reconstruct a rule from first principles.

This is also the honest answer to the question of whether six weeks of tuition before an exam will help. Content teaching can be compressed. Fluency cannot. A student who still pauses over index laws in March of DP2 will pause over them in the examination, and the useful plan at that point is to protect the marks that are reachable rather than to attempt a rebuild that needs a term. A tutor who takes a late booking should say which of those two plans they are selling.

Where a family does have time, the pattern that works in Al Ain is unglamorous. A fixed weekly session, ten minutes of unassisted arithmetic at the start of every one, a short set between sessions marked before the next, and a recorded running score on those ten-minute sets so improvement is visible to the student rather than asserted by an adult. Families who can see the line moving stay with the plan; families who are only told it is working tend to stop in February.

sections.heading: The five topics at Standard Level, and the fault that recurs in each
paragraphs: Analysis and Approaches SL is organised into five topics: number and algebra, functions, geometry and trigonometry, statistics and probability, and calculus. Marks are not lost evenly across them, and they are not lost randomly inside them. Each topic has a characteristic failure that shows up again and again in Al Ain scripts, and naming it is usually more useful than re-teaching the topic from the top.

The table below lists those faults. They are worth reading alongside a marked script, because a parent who can see that three of their child's lost marks are the same radian error twice and one sign slip has a much clearer picture than one who has been told the student needs to work harder on trigonometry. Specific faults also make the tuition plan short: a radian habit can be fixed in two sessions, while a genuine gap in the calculus block takes a term.

One pattern cuts across all five topics. Students who have been taught to check an answer by substituting it back into the original expression lose fewer marks than students who check by redoing the calculation the same way. The second method repeats the original error; the first catches it. That habit costs nothing to install and is the closest thing to free marks available in a Standard Level paper.

The other cross-cutting issue is presentation of method. The published mark schemes award method marks for recognisable steps, and a student who writes a single line and a final answer forfeits those even when the answer is right. In Paper 2 this becomes expensive, because a calculator produces an answer in one move and the student has nothing on the page to support it. Writing the function being solved, the window or limits used, and the quantity being read off is a two-line habit that protects several marks per paper.

sections.heading: The exploration: twenty marks across five criteria
paragraphs: The mathematical exploration is 20 per cent of the Standard Level grade and runs to between 12 and 20 pages. It is marked out of 20 against five criteria, and the mark allocations are uneven in a way that changes how a student should spend their time. Use of mathematics carries the largest single block of marks, presentation and mathematical communication carry four each, and personal engagement and reflection carry three each. A student who spends three weeks on formatting and two days on the mathematics has misread the rubric.

At Standard Level the commonest reason an exploration underscores is topic choice rather than writing quality. A topic that forces mathematics above the course leaves the student explaining a technique they do not control, which costs marks under use of mathematics and under communication at the same time. A topic that only needs GCSE-level work caps the same criterion from below. The viability check is therefore the highest-value hour of supervision available, and it happens before any writing, not after a draft exists.

Reflection is the criterion most often left until the end, and it is the one that most clearly cannot be retrofitted. Marks here go to reflection that is critical and developed through the work, which means a student noticing partway through that a model does not fit, saying so, and doing something about it. A closing paragraph about what was enjoyable scores at the bottom of the band. A tutor can teach what that looks like by showing where in a piece of work the opportunity existed.

The boundary on this work is firm and it is in the student's interest. The exploration must be the student's own from first page to last. A tutor reads a draft and responds with questions: what does this notation mean, why this model, what happens at the boundary, where is the reflection on the choice you made on page four. A tutor who returns replacement sentences or supplies the mathematics has put the student at risk of a malpractice finding, which is a far worse outcome than a middling mark honestly earned.

sections.heading: Coverage for this course in Al Ain, and what happens when nobody is free
paragraphs: Al Ain has a smaller pool of Diploma-specific maths teaching than Abu Dhabi island or Dubai, and that is the honest starting point. Standard Level Analysis and Approaches is the most widely covered Diploma maths course we handle, so a match is usually straightforward. The constraint is rarely the subject; it is the slot. A family that needs a fixed Sunday at half past five in October has a narrower set of options than a family that can take seven o'clock on a Tuesday, and the second family will be matched faster.

Where a request is for something narrower, we say so before taking a booking. Exploration supervision through to a school deadline needs a tutor who has done it before and has capacity in that specific fortnight. A combined request, such as one tutor covering both this course and Physics SL, narrows the pool considerably and is often better served by two specialists than by one generalist who is adequate at both.

If no suitable tutor is free at a family's time, there are three honest answers and we use whichever is true: a different slot with the right specialist, a short wait with a date attached, or a tutor based outside the UAE teaching the same syllabus on Gulf Standard Time. The third option is how most niche Diploma requests get covered anywhere in the UAE, and families are entitled to be told that is what is happening rather than discovering it in the first lesson. What we do not do is accept the booking and allocate whoever is available.

Market context helps a family judge quotes. Published rate information in this market, read in October 2026, puts budget online tuition from roughly AED 45 to 65 an hour on provider rate cards, qualified subject tutors around AED 150 to 300, IB and IGCSE specialists around AED 200 to 450 and above, and premium named tutors quoted as high as AED 650, with in-home visits carrying a travel premium of their own. Those are market figures from providers' own published pages and from Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 table, not our price list, and any quote should be checked against them.

sections.heading: What a tutor may do on assessed work, and what nobody should offer
paragraphs: The IB treats authorship seriously, and the consequences of getting this wrong fall on the student rather than on the tutor. Work submitted for assessment has to be the student's own, and a student whose exploration contains material supplied by someone else is exposed to a malpractice investigation that can cost the Diploma. Any tutoring arrangement that sounds easier than the honest one is selling the family a risk it has not been told about.

What a tutor legitimately does is teach, question and give feedback. Teaching the mathematics a student needs in order to attempt a topic is support. Checking at the outset whether a chosen topic can carry Standard Level mathematics is support. Reading a draft and returning questions about notation, structure, assumptions and the missing reflection is support. Explaining the criteria with their mark allocations, so the student can see which of their own weaknesses costs most, is support.

What a tutor does not do is produce the work. That means no supplied paragraphs, no corrected text handed back as a replacement, no calculations performed on the student's behalf and dropped into their document, and nothing resembling a completed piece of coursework in any form. One competitor in this market advertises finished internal assessments for sale. That is an academic-integrity breach, it is an expulsion risk for the student, and it is the clearest line in the whole subject.

Parents can hold a tutor to this with one question: show me what you returned on the last draft you read. An honest answer is a page of questions and annotations in the margin. A page of rewritten mathematics is the wrong answer, however good it looks, and a family is better off knowing that before a school deadline than after a coordinator asks the student to explain their own page four.

sections.heading: Fitting a maths session to the Al Ain school week
paragraphs: Scheduling is the quiet reason tuition plans fail, and Al Ain has its own version of the problem. Private schools in the emirate are licensed and inspected by ADEK, and most follow the Ministry's unified academic calendar: three terms running from late August to early July, with a winter break around the turn of the year and a spring break in late March. Individual campuses publish their own dates and some run an alternative calendar, so the family's own school diary is the document that matters, not a general rule.

Inside that year, two windows do most of the damage to a maths plan. The first is the overlap in DP1 between the calculus block and the opening exploration deadlines, which lands in the same weeks at most Al Ain schools and leaves students trying to learn new technique while drafting independent work. The second is the mock season in DP2, when a student discovers their Paper 1 reliability for the first time under real conditions and often wants to double the session count in the worst possible month.

Ramadan changes the shape of the week rather than cancelling it. School hours shorten, energy drops in the afternoon, and the sessions that still work are the ones moved to after iftar. We reschedule rather than skip, because a six-week gap in unassisted arithmetic is visible afterwards in a way a six-week gap in content teaching is not. Families who plan the shift in advance lose nothing; families who improvise usually lose the slot.

Online delivery is what makes those moves possible. All UAE lessons run one to one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, so a slot can shift by ninety minutes without anyone recalculating a drive across Al Ain at the end of a school day. IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE: our in-home service exists only in India. For a Standard Level maths student in Zakher or Al Foah, the practical consequence is that the tutor is chosen for knowing where Paper 1 marks go, not for living on the right side of the city.

process.description: One hour a week on Gulf Standard Time, sequenced against the school's scheme of work and its exploration deadlines rather than a generic syllabus order. Ten minutes of unassisted arithmetic sits in every session from the first week, not from the final term.

process.description: Progress is read from the marked sets and the no-calculator scores, which both student and parent can see, with a review point agreed at the start. If the line is flat after a fair run, we change the tutor or the plan rather than adding hours to the same arrangement.

whyPoints.title: The route question answered before hours are sold
whyPoints.description: We teach all four Diploma maths courses, so there is nothing to protect in saying a student is in the wrong one. On an Al Ain timetable, where a second Standard Level route may not run at all, that answer is worth more than a term of tuition against the wrong problem.

whyPoints.title: Paper 1 treated as its own skill
whyPoints.description: Unassisted arithmetic and algebra are trainable and slow to build, so they start in the first session rather than in the final term. Ten minutes a week for six months moves more Standard Level marks than two more topics covered at speed.

whyPoints.title: Matched on the topic, not on the subject label
whyPoints.description: Before a family books, we name the topic the tutor is strongest in and say whether they have supervised explorations to submission. A tutor who is good at calculus and vague about statistics is the right match for one student and the wrong one for another.

whyPoints.description: A tutor teaches, questions and gives feedback on the student's own work, and produces none of it. We put that in writing before a supervision block starts, because the risk of getting it wrong falls on the student and on nobody else.

whyPoints.description: Al Ain sits in the Emirate of Abu Dhabi, so private schools here answer to ADEK rather than to Dubai's KHDA. Writing that correctly is a small thing that tells a parent whether the rest of the page was written for their city or for a search engine.

faqs.question: Is Analysis and Approaches SL the right maths course for my child, or should they be in Applications and Interpretation?
faqs.answer: Watch them work through a past Paper 1 for forty minutes. A student suited to Analysis and Approaches starts each question, sets up a method and sometimes loses the thread in the algebra. A student better suited to Applications and Interpretation often does not start, because the opening move is an algebraic manipulation they were never fluent in, yet comes alive in front of a data set or a model. The content lists differ concretely too: Analysis and Approaches carries the binomial theorem, logarithms and real calculus, while Applications and Interpretation adds the chi-squared test, financial mathematics and Voronoi diagrams. In Al Ain the deciding factor is often whether the school timetables both routes at all.

faqs.question: Why is Paper 1 so much harder for my child than Paper 2 when the topics are the same?
faqs.answer: Because Paper 1 permits no calculator of any kind and Paper 2 requires one throughout. In Paper 2 a student who understands the shape of a problem can reach the answer by solving numerically, finding an intersection or reading an inverse normal value. In Paper 1 that same understanding earns nothing unless exact values, surd and index laws, log rules and clean factorising are available from memory at speed. A large gap between the two papers almost always means an unfinished IGCSE or MYP algebra habit that a calculator has been concealing, not a problem with Diploma mathematics itself. It responds to short, frequent, unassisted practice rather than to more content teaching.

faqs.question: How are the two papers and the exploration combined into a Standard Level maths grade?
faqs.answer: Analysis and Approaches SL has three assessed components. Paper 1 runs 1 hour 30 minutes for 80 marks and carries 40 per cent of the grade. Paper 2 runs 1 hour 30 minutes for 80 marks and carries another 40 per cent. The mathematical exploration carries the remaining 20 per cent and is marked out of 20. Both papers are divided into a short-response Section A and an extended-response Section B, and the formula booklet is supplied in both. The practical consequence is that a fifth of the grade is decided before the examination room, on work a student does over several months, which is the part of the course most families underestimate.

faqs.question: My daughter is in DP1 and wants to move up to Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level. Is that realistic in Al Ain?
faqs.answer: It depends far more on the timetable than on her ability. Higher Level adds ninety guided hours, proof by induction, complex numbers, three-dimensional vectors and differential equations, plus a one-hour Paper 3 worth a fifth of the grade. Al Ain Diploma cohorts are small, and many schools cannot run Analysis and Approaches at both levels in the same option block, so the move may require a timetable change rather than a class change. Raise it with the Diploma coordinator in DP1 while options are still movable. A specialist can tell you from a script whether the content step is manageable; only the school can tell you whether the slot exists.

faqs.question: What should a Standard Level maths exploration actually be about?
faqs.answer: Something the student can carry with mathematics at the level of their own course. The commonest cause of a low mark at Standard Level is topic choice, not writing. A topic that needs techniques above the syllabus forces the student to explain mathematics they do not control, which costs marks under use of mathematics and under communication at the same time. A topic that only needs GCSE-level work caps the same criterion from below. Good Standard Level topics usually start from something the student measures, models or already argues about, and the viability check belongs at the start, before weeks of work, rather than after a draft exists.

faqs.question: How many marks is each exploration criterion worth?
faqs.answer: Twenty marks in total across five criteria. Presentation carries four, mathematical communication carries four, personal engagement carries three, reflection carries three and use of mathematics carries six. The allocation should change how a student spends their time: the single largest block sits on the mathematics itself, while formatting, which absorbs the most anxiety, is worth four. Reflection is the criterion that cannot be added at the end, because the marks go to critical reflection developed through the work rather than to a closing paragraph about what was enjoyable. Ask your child which criterion they think is weakest; if they cannot name one, nobody has explained the rubric to them.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help with the exploration without putting my son at risk?
faqs.answer: Yes, within a firm boundary. A tutor may teach the mathematics needed to attempt the topic, check at the outset whether the topic can carry Standard Level mathematics, explain the criteria with their mark allocations, and read a draft and respond with questions about notation, assumptions, structure and missing reflection. A tutor may not supply paragraphs, hand back rewritten mathematics, perform calculations that then appear in the document, or deliver anything resembling finished coursework. The work has to be the student's own, and a malpractice finding falls on him rather than on anyone else. One test for any tutor: ask to see what they returned on the last draft they read.

faqs.question: We have ten weeks until the mock exams. What is the best use of them for Standard Level maths?
faqs.answer: Protecting reachable marks rather than attempting a rebuild. Content can be compressed into ten weeks; fluency cannot, so a student who still hesitates over index laws will hesitate over them in the examination. A realistic ten-week plan does three things: it fixes the cheap recurring faults, such as radians left off in Paper 2 and missing constants of integration, it drills the specific topics that appear reliably in Section A, and it installs the habit of writing enough method that correct answers attract their method marks. A tutor taking a late booking should tell you which plan they are selling, because the honest one is narrower than the hopeful one.

faqs.question: Do universities in the UAE and abroad insist on Analysis and Approaches rather than Applications and Interpretation?
faqs.answer: Published entry requirements name Analysis and Approaches more often for mathematics-facing degrees such as engineering, physics, mathematics and some economics programmes. It is a pattern rather than a rule: it varies between institutions, between courses within one institution, and between admissions cycles. Business, psychology, design, architecture and most social science routes commonly accept either course. The only safe method is to read the requirement on the specific programme's own admissions page for the year of entry, including for Al Ain's own institutions, and to do it before the DP1 option form goes back rather than in DP2. Do not take a route requirement from any tutoring site, this one included.

faqs.question: Which body regulates private schools in Al Ain, and does it decide which maths courses are offered?
faqs.answer: Al Ain is part of the Emirate of Abu Dhabi, so its private schools come under ADEK, the Department of Education and Knowledge, which supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate. Dubai's KHDA has no role here, and pages that tell an Al Ain family otherwise were not written for them. Which Diploma maths courses a school offers is a school decision shaped by cohort size and staffing rather than a regulator instruction, which is why a small Al Ain Diploma cohort often runs one Standard Level route rather than two. The regulator governs licensing, inspection and curriculum approval, not your child's option block.

faqs.question: Does a private maths tutor in Al Ain need a permit, and can we ask to see it?
faqs.answer: Yes, and yes. Private tuition in the UAE runs on a MoHRE private tutor work permit, introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023. It is granted free of charge for two years, and eligible applicants include registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Anyone offering private tutoring without one is subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and no fine schedule has been published, so treat any specific amount you read with caution. Asking a tutor directly about their permit is reasonable and normal. Abu Dhabi's ethics rules also bar school staff from tutoring students enrolled at their own school.

faqs.question: Is online maths tuition genuinely as useful as someone sitting at the table?
faqs.answer: For this course, the format that matters is a shared writing surface, and online lessons have one. Standard Level maths teaching is watching a student attempt a manipulation and intervening at the exact moment the method goes wrong, which works on a shared whiteboard where both people write and the script stays afterwards for the student to revisit. IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE; every UAE lesson is one-to-one teaching over live video on Gulf Standard Time. What a family in Al Ain gains in exchange is a tutor chosen for knowing where Paper 1 marks go, instead of whoever could reach the house by five o'clock on a school day.

faqs.question: What do private maths tutors charge in this market, and what should we expect to pay?
faqs.answer: Published figures read in October 2026 give a usable range. Provider rate cards advertise budget online tuition from roughly AED 45 to 65 an hour, qualified subject tutors sit around AED 150 to 300, IB and IGCSE specialists around AED 200 to 450 and above, and premium named tutors have been quoted as high as AED 650. In-home visits carry a travel premium on top, which is why monthly in-home packages in this market run well above online ones. Those are market figures from providers' own pages and from Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 table, not our price list. Ask any provider for the rate in AED per 60 minutes and whether it includes marking.

faqs.question: Can lessons move during Ramadan and the mock season without losing the plan?
faqs.answer: Yes, and the shift should be planned rather than improvised. School hours shorten during Ramadan and afternoon energy drops, so the sessions that work are the ones moved to after iftar. We reschedule rather than pause, because a six-week break in unassisted arithmetic shows up afterwards in a way that a break in content teaching does not. The mock season is the opposite problem: families want to double the session count in the busiest month. The better answer is usually two shorter sessions a week rather than one long one, with timed sections marked against the published mark scheme wording instead of a tick for the right answer.

faqs.question: What happens if there is no Analysis and Approaches specialist free at the time we need?
faqs.answer: You get one of three honest answers. A different hour with the right specialist, which is the commonest fix and usually a question of moving by ninety minutes. A short wait with an actual date attached. Or a tutor based outside the UAE who teaches the same syllabus on Gulf Standard Time, which is how most niche Diploma requests are covered anywhere in this country. You are entitled to be told which of those three applies before you book, rather than finding out in the first lesson. What does not happen is a booking accepted and then filled with whoever happened to be available that week.

faqs.question: My son came through Cambridge IGCSE with a grade 8 in maths. Why is Standard Level going badly?
faqs.answer: Because IGCSE permits a calculator in the papers that matter and Analysis and Approaches SL Paper 1 does not. A strong IGCSE grade can be built while leaning on a calculator for arithmetic, taking partial credit on algebraic fractions and avoiding questions that need completing the square. Paper 1 removes all three shelters at once, often in the first DP1 mock. The gap is usually fluency rather than understanding: expanding and factorising on sight, index and surd laws in both directions, rearranging a formula where the subject appears twice. It is fixable with short, frequent, unassisted practice, but it takes months rather than weeks, which is why it is worth starting in DP1.

al-ain/ib-dp-physics-hl-tutor.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach Diploma Programme Physics at Higher Level to students in Al Ain and across the Emirate of Abu Dhabi. Each one is matched to a named theme, a named paper and a named deadline before the trial lesson is booked, so the first hour is spent on your child's actual gap.

intro.heading: Where your child is now, and what the weeks between here and the May session look like
paragraphs: An IB DP Physics HL tutor in Al Ain is answering a timeline question, not a subject question. A parent rarely searches this phrase because they want a general overview of Higher Level Physics. They search it because a predicted grade has landed lower than the university offer needs, because the scientific investigation draft came back with a weak Evaluation mark, or because Theme D arrived and the student stopped understanding lessons they used to follow. The useful first question is not what Physics HL covers. It is how many teaching weeks are left, and what has to happen inside them.

The Diploma is a two-year course with a Higher Level subject allocation of 240 guided teaching hours, and almost every recoverable problem in Physics HL is a sequencing problem. Kinematics and forces in Theme A are taught early, assessed lightly in DP1, then relied on constantly in Theme C and Theme D a year later. A student who never fully fixed vector resolution in October of DP1 will meet the same gap again in the autumn of DP2 wearing a different costume: as circular motion, as the component of a gravitational field along a slope, as a flux calculation. Finding the original gap is what makes a term of tutoring different from a term of re-teaching.

Al Ain adds a specific constraint. The city is part of the Emirate of Abu Dhabi, so its private schools are licensed and inspected by ADEK, the Department of Education and Knowledge, which supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate. The inland school set is smaller than the capital's, and Higher Level sciences are where that shows. A cohort of eight Physics HL students in one Al Ain school is normal. One teacher may carry both the SL and HL sets in the same room, which is workable for Theme A and much harder for the HL-only material in A.4, A.5, B.4, D.4 and E.2.

What a tutor can honestly offer against that is time and specialisation, not proximity. Lessons here are delivered online, one-to-one, over live video. IB Gram does not run in-home visits anywhere in the UAE; home visits are a service offered only in India. The trade is deliberate. A family in Al Ain gets a Physics HL specialist who has taught the current guide and marked work against the current investigation criteria, instead of whichever tutor is willing to drive 130 kilometres from Abu Dhabi island on a Tuesday evening.

The rest of this page is laid out as a countdown. It starts with what the course actually contains and what the HL-only additions are, moves through the assessment weightings and the places marks are lost, sets out the investigation criteria and their mark allocations, and then works backwards from the May session through every internal deadline a DP student in Al Ain meets on the way. The AED rate bands, the permit position and the ADEK context sit at the end, because they are decisions a parent makes once and the teaching plan is the thing that changes week to week.
bullets: Higher Level Physics is assessed by two papers and one internal investigation, weighted 36%, 44% and 20%
The HL-only material is concentrated in rigid body mechanics, relativity, thermodynamics, induction and quantum physics
A 3,000-word limit applies to the scientific investigation report, marked out of 24 across four criteria
Al Ain private schools sit under ADEK, not KHDA, so inspection reports and policies come from a different authority
Sessions are live online and timed to Gulf Standard Time; there is no in-home option in the UAE

al-ain/ib-dp-physics-hl-tutor.programmesIntro: Four routes bring an Al Ain student to this page, and each one starts the countdown at a different point. The notes below say what the gap usually is at each stage and how long it typically takes to close in weekly one-to-one sessions.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme Physics, Higher Level
programmes.ageRange: Ages 16-19 · DP1 and DP2 · 240 guided hours
programmes.description: The full Higher Level course: the five themes plus the HL-only extensions, two written papers and the scientific investigation. Paper 1 is split into a multiple-choice section and a data-analysis section; Paper 2 carries the long structured and extended-response questions. The data booklet is supplied in the examination, which changes what is worth memorising and what is worth practising.
programmes.countryNote: In Al Ain the HL set is often small enough to share a room with the SL set. That means the HL-only topics are frequently taught in compressed blocks late in DP2, and a student who misses two weeks of D.4 induction through illness or travel has no second pass through it at school. Weekly one-to-one sessions exist mainly to hold that material open.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme Physics, Standard Level
programmes.ageRange: Ages 16-19 · DP1 and DP2 · 150 guided hours
programmes.description: The same five themes without the Higher Level extensions, shorter papers and the same investigation worth 20%. Standard Level students who are considering a move up to Higher Level need the decision made early, because the HL additions are not evenly spread across the two years and catching up on A.4 and A.5 in DP2 is a different task from meeting them in sequence.
programmes.countryNote: Al Ain students sometimes start Physics at Standard Level because the HL set did not run, then need Higher Level for an engineering application to a UK or UAE university. Where a school can accommodate the switch, the realistic window is the first term of DP1. We will say plainly when a switch is no longer sensible rather than sell sessions against it.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme Sciences, Years 4 and 5
programmes.description: MYP Sciences is assessed on four criteria and rewards investigation design and communication. Diploma Physics rewards algebraic fluency, unit discipline and the ability to read a graph gradient as a physical quantity. The gap between the two is the single most common reason a strong MYP student finds DP1 Physics harder than expected in the first term.
programmes.countryNote: Al Ain families moving from an MYP programme into a Diploma set in the same school still cross this gap, and so do students arriving from a British Year 11 or a CBSE Class 10. The pre-DP summer is the cheapest time to close it: six to eight sessions on rearranging formulae, logarithms, trigonometry in context and uncertainty notation.

programmes.name: Physics Extended Essay and the Theory of Knowledge link
programmes.description: A Physics Extended Essay needs a question narrow enough to answer with data a student can actually gather. Supervision here means process coaching: reading the research question for feasibility, checking that the method generates enough data points, questioning the uncertainty treatment, and reviewing the student's own drafts against the published criteria.
programmes.countryNote: A tutor working with an Al Ain student on a Physics Extended Essay never produces text for it. The school supervisor signs the authenticity declaration, and the IB treats work that is not the student's own as malpractice. What a tutor adds is feasibility pressure early, when a research question is still changeable, and honest criticism of the student's own analysis later.

al-ain/ib-dp-physics-hl-tutor.subjectsIntro: The grid below is the Physics Higher Level course as a tutoring plan rather than a syllabus listing. Each entry names what the theme assesses and where Al Ain students most often lose marks on it, so a trial lesson can start somewhere specific.

subjects.name: Theme A: Space, time and motion
subjects.levels: SL and HL, with A.4 and A.5 Higher Level only
subjects.description: Kinematics, forces, momentum, work, energy and power at both levels, then rigid body mechanics and Galilean and special relativity for Higher Level. Marks go missing on vector resolution, on momentum problems where the system boundary is chosen carelessly, and on relativity questions where the student picks the wrong frame before doing any algebra.

subjects.name: Theme B: The particulate nature of matter
subjects.levels: SL and HL, with B.4 Higher Level only
subjects.description: Thermal energy transfers, the greenhouse effect, gas laws and current and circuits, plus thermodynamics for Higher Level. The usual losses are specific heat capacity questions answered without tracking which body gains and which loses, circuit questions where internal resistance is ignored, and entropy answers that describe disorder instead of using the definition.

subjects.name: Theme C: Wave behaviour
subjects.description: Simple harmonic motion, the wave model, wave phenomena, standing waves and resonance, and the Doppler effect. Higher Level pushes further into single-slit and multiple-slit interference and quantitative Doppler treatment. Students who never secured phase relationships in simple harmonic motion lose marks across the whole theme rather than in one place.

subjects.name: Theme D: Fields
subjects.levels: SL and HL, with D.4 Higher Level only
subjects.description: Gravitational fields, electric and magnetic fields, motion in electromagnetic fields, and electromagnetic induction for Higher Level. This is where Al Ain HL students most often report that lessons stopped making sense, because the theme assumes fluent vector work and comfort with inverse-square relationships from Theme A a year earlier.

subjects.name: Theme E: Nuclear and quantum physics
subjects.levels: SL and HL, with E.2 Higher Level only
subjects.description: Atomic structure, radioactive decay, fission, fusion and stars at both levels, with quantum physics added at Higher Level. Taught late in DP2, so it is the theme most often compressed. Mass-energy calculations lose marks on unit conversion more often than on physics, and stellar questions lose them on reading a Hertzsprung-Russell diagram.

subjects.name: The scientific investigation
subjects.levels: SL and HL, 20% of the final mark
subjects.description: One report of up to 3,000 words, marked out of 24 across Research design, Data analysis, Conclusion and Evaluation. Evaluation is the criterion where UAE students most often leave marks behind, because it asks for method-specific weaknesses and realistic improvements rather than general statements about human error and more repeats.

subjects.name: Paper 1B data analysis
subjects.description: The data-based section of Paper 1 asks students to process unfamiliar experimental data: plot, linearise, read a gradient, assign uncertainty, and comment on whether the data support a relationship. It is the most trainable part of the whole course and the part most often left untrained until the final weeks.

subjects.name: Paper 2 extended response
subjects.description: Long structured questions that cross themes inside a single scenario, where command terms decide the mark. Explain, describe, outline, determine, deduce and justify each ask for a different shape of answer, and a correct physics answer written to the wrong command term still loses the mark.

subjects.name: Mathematics AA alongside Physics HL
subjects.description: Physics HL leans on calculus, logarithms and trigonometric manipulation that Mathematics AA covers directly. Students taking Mathematics AI alongside Physics HL are not disadvantaged by the IB, but they usually need the algebraic fluency built deliberately rather than picked up in the maths lesson.

subjects.name: Physics Extended Essay
subjects.description: A 4,000-word independent investigation with its own criteria and its own supervision rules. The common failure is a research question that cannot be answered with the data available in a school laboratory, discovered too late to change. Feasibility pressure in the first fortnight is worth more than any amount of editing later.

sections.heading: What an IB DP Physics HL tutor in Al Ain is actually being asked to fix
paragraphs: Three problems account for most searches for an IB DP Physics HL tutor in Al Ain. The first is a predicted grade that sits below a university offer, usually discovered in DP1 reports or at the start of DP2. The second is the scientific investigation, where a student has collected data that does not support the relationship they expected and has six weeks to turn it into a report marked out of 24. The third is a specific theme, almost always Theme D fields or the Higher Level thermodynamics in B.4, where the student can follow worked examples in class and cannot start a question alone.

Each of those needs a different plan, and the distinction matters because the cheapest mistake a family makes is booking open-ended weekly sessions for a problem that has a finish point. A predicted-grade problem is a sequencing problem and takes a term. An investigation problem is a four-to-six-hour block timed to specific deadlines. A single-theme problem is three to five sessions and then stops. Selling a term of tuition for a three-session problem is how tutoring gets its reputation in this city.

The diagnostic that separates them is simple and happens in the trial lesson. The student attempts two past-paper questions on the topic they say is the problem, talking through what they are doing. If they cannot start, the gap is prerequisite and sits earlier in the course. If they start correctly and lose marks at the end, the gap is command-term and exam-technique work. If they produce correct physics and the wrong quantity, the gap is unit and notation discipline, which is the fastest of the three to fix and the most commonly misdiagnosed as a content problem.
bullets: Cannot start the question: the gap is earlier in the course, not in this theme
Starts correctly, loses the final marks: command terms and answer structure
Correct method, wrong quantity: units, prefixes and significant figures
Correct everything, too slow: timing practice rather than more teaching

sections.heading: The Higher Level course, theme by theme, and what the HL-only material adds
paragraphs: The current IB Physics guide organises content into five themes rather than the older topic-and-option structure, and the Higher Level course is the Standard Level content plus a set of named extensions. Knowing exactly where those extensions sit matters for planning, because they are not spread evenly across the two years. A student who joins Higher Level late, or who misses a block of DP2 through travel, loses a disproportionate share of the HL-only material rather than a slice of everything.

The table below maps the five themes to their Higher Level additions. The right-hand column is the planning answer: how much extra tutoring time that extension usually needs for a student who is secure on the Standard Level content underneath it. Those figures are our own teaching estimate for one-to-one sessions, not a published IB figure, and a student weak on the prerequisites needs more.

One pattern is worth naming before the table. Theme A is the prerequisite for Theme C and Theme D, and Theme B's circuits material is the prerequisite for the induction work in D.4. This is why a Physics HL student in Al Ain who struggled quietly in the first term of DP1 tends to hit a visible wall in the autumn of DP2. The wall is not Theme D. It is Theme A, met again at a level that no longer tolerates approximation.

The guide also sets out a tools and inquiry strand that runs through every theme rather than sitting in one of them: experimental technique, use of technology, and the mathematics a physicist is expected to apply without prompting. Schools teach it inside practical work, which means it is rarely revised as a topic and rarely tested as one until Paper 1B arrives. For an Al Ain student in a small Higher Level set, that strand is often the quietest gap on the page, because nobody has ever marked it separately.

sections.heading: How Higher Level Physics is assessed, and where the marks go
paragraphs: Higher Level Physics is assessed by two written papers and one internal investigation. Paper 1 carries 36% of the grade and is split into a multiple-choice section and a data-analysis section. Paper 2 carries 44% and holds the structured and extended-response questions. The scientific investigation carries the remaining 20%. A parent reading a report that says Physics is going fine is reading an opinion about Paper 2 performance; the other 56% of the grade is often not being tested at school at all until late.

That weighting has a direct consequence for how tutoring hours are spent. Paper 1B data analysis is a trainable skill with a small syllabus: plot, linearise, read a gradient as a physical quantity, propagate uncertainty, and judge whether the data support the claimed relationship. A student can move several marks on it in four or five focused sessions. The same hours spent on general content revision move far less, because content knowledge is usually not the binding constraint by the spring of DP2.

The investigation is the other asymmetry. It is 20% of the grade, it is marked out of 24 by the school and moderated by the IB, and it is the only component where the student controls the conditions completely. A mark of 18 rather than 12 on the investigation is worth more to a final grade than most students' realistic gain on Paper 2 in the same number of weeks. Families who understand this book the investigation clinic in DP1 and the exam block in DP2, in that order.

sections.heading: The scientific investigation, criterion by criterion, with its mark allocations
paragraphs: The scientific investigation is one report of up to 3,000 words, marked out of 24 across four criteria: Research design, Data analysis, Conclusion and Evaluation, each carrying 6 marks. No competitor page on this search names a single criterion or a single mark allocation, and parents are routinely asked to support a component they have never seen described. The breakdown below is what the student is actually being marked against.

Research design is where most recoverable marks sit, and it is decided before any data exists. A research question that names the independent variable, the dependent variable and the range, with a method that controls the obvious confounders and generates enough data points to plot, is most of the criterion. A question like whether temperature affects resistance is not answerable at this level; the same investigation framed around resistance against temperature over a stated range with a stated number of readings is.

Evaluation is where UAE students most often lose marks, and the reason is consistent. The criterion asks for weaknesses specific to this method and improvements that would actually address them. Writing that human error affected the results, or that more repeats would help, describes any experiment ever conducted and earns little. Writing that the thermometer's resolution limited the temperature readings to the nearest half degree, which accounts for the scatter at the low end, and that a thermocouple with data logging would reduce it, is the same length and earns the mark.

sections.heading: The May session counted backwards: a twenty-four month plan from DP1 to results day
paragraphs: Diploma students in Al Ain sit the May session, as do almost all UAE schools. The table below is deliberately expressed in windows relative to that session rather than in calendar dates. IB examination and results dates are set by the IB and published through ibo.org and the school's Diploma coordinator, and dates found on tutoring sites are frequently out of date, so the authoritative source for your child's cohort is the coordinator's own calendar.

What the table does give is the shape of the two years, which does not change. Subject choices and Higher Level decisions are made before DP1 begins. The investigation is proposed, run and written across DP1 term 3 and DP2 term 1. Internal deadlines for the Extended Essay and the investigation cluster in the autumn of DP2, which is also when Theme D and Theme E are being taught. That overlap is the single busiest point in the course and it is predictable eighteen months in advance.

Reading the table backwards is the useful direction for a parent who has just arrived at this page in the spring of DP2. If the investigation is already submitted and the papers are the remaining problem, the realistic plan is a six-to-ten week intensive block built from the student's own scripts. If the investigation is still open, that comes first regardless of how the papers look, because it is 20% of the grade under the student's own control and the papers are not.

sections.heading: What Physics tutoring costs in Al Ain and across the Emirate of Abu Dhabi
paragraphs: Published rates for IB tutoring in the UAE are scarce, and the pages that do publish them usually quote in dollars. The bands below are market rates gathered from providers' own published pricing and from Bestimate's 2026 tutoring cost survey for Dubai. They are what the market charges, not an IB Gram price list. Our own pricing is quoted after the free trial lesson, against the subject, the level and the number of weeks left, because a four-session investigation block and a two-year weekly booking are not the same product.

Two things are specific to Al Ain. In-home rates in the city carry the same travel loading as the capital without the same supply of Higher Level science specialists, so a family paying the top of the in-home band is frequently paying a travel premium for a tutor who teaches Standard Level content confidently and Higher Level content from a textbook. Online rates do not carry the travel loading, which is most of the gap between the two columns below.

The other Al Ain factor is scarcity rather than price. A Physics HL specialist who has taught the current guide, marked investigations against the current criteria and worked through a full Paper 2 series is not a common find within driving distance of Al Jimi. The honest comparison is not cheaper against more expensive. It is a subject specialist at an online rate against a generalist at an in-home rate, and for Higher Level Physics in the final year that difference shows up in the marks.

sections.heading: Online sessions against a tutor driving to a villa in Zakher
paragraphs: The phrase most Al Ain parents start with is home tuition, and it deserves a straight answer rather than a redirect. In-home tutoring in Al Ain is a real market. It is priced at roughly AED 180-500 an hour depending on level and tutor, according to the market sources above, and a substantial part of that is travel. A tutor crossing Al Ain between Zakher and Al Jimi in the late afternoon is giving up a working hour to do it, and that hour is in the rate whether it is itemised or not.

IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE. Lessons for Al Ain families are delivered online, one-to-one, over live video, and in-home tutoring is a service we run only in India. The comparison below is the honest case for that choice rather than a dismissal of the alternative. For Higher Level Physics specifically, the deciding factor is the size of the available tutor pool: online, the pool is every Physics HL specialist who can teach at a Gulf Standard Time evening slot, which is a different order of magnitude from those within a 20-minute drive of a particular Al Ain district.

There are genuine advantages on the other side and it is dishonest to pretend otherwise. A younger student who needs supervision as much as teaching is often better served face to face. A student who will not engage with a screen will not learn from one. For a DP2 Physics HL student working through past papers on a shared document with a tutor annotating the same script in real time, the screen is not a compromise; it is a better tool than two people and one piece of paper.

sections.heading: ADEK, the private tutor permit, and how to check your child's tutor is legal
paragraphs: Al Ain sits in the Emirate of Abu Dhabi, so its private schools are licensed and inspected by ADEK, the Department of Education and Knowledge, which supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate. This is a different authority from Dubai's KHDA, and it matters in practice: inspection reports, policy circulars and staff conduct rules for an Al Ain campus come from ADEK, and a tutoring page that explains Dubai's KHDA framework to an Al Ain parent is explaining the wrong regulator.

Private tutoring itself is regulated federally through MoHRE. The private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, it is granted free of charge for two years, and eligible applicants include teachers registered in government or private schools, employees in the government and private sectors, unemployed individuals, school students aged 15 to 18 and university students. Individuals offering private tutoring without a permit from MoHRE are subject to fines and penalties outlined in the applicable laws. No fine schedule has been published, so any page quoting a figure is guessing.

One Abu Dhabi rule deserves particular attention from Al Ain parents. ADEK's professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff have been reported to prohibit teachers from providing paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, and the MoHRE permit's code of conduct has been reported to bar the same thing. Verify the current wording against ADEK's own policy document before relying on it, but treat an offer of your child's own classroom teacher for paid private lessons as a question worth asking rather than a convenience. IB Gram holds no ADEK, MoHRE or IB accreditation and claims none; what we can do is tell you what to ask.

sections.heading: If the Physics grade decides a medicine or engineering application
paragraphs: Higher Level Physics is a prerequisite rather than a preference for a large share of engineering courses, and it is a common third subject in science applications. That changes what a tutoring plan is for. A student who needs a 6 to hold an offer is in a different position from one who needs a 4 to pass the Diploma, and the sections of the course worth hours are different. A borderline 5-to-6 student usually gains most from Paper 1B and command-term work; a borderline 3-to-4 student gains most from securing Theme A and Theme B properly.

For students staying in the UAE, the Ministry of Education equivalency process is a separate matter from the university's own entry requirements, and no tutoring provider performs or guarantees it. For British-track students, the published requirements are five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates with a grade of no less than E or grade 3, excluding Arabic and Islamic education from that count, plus one accredited subject at Advanced Level with a grade of no less than E or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade. For the American track, English proficiency is a score of 5 in IELTS academic, 61 in TOEFL iBT or 450 in SAT reading and writing, and mathematics requires at least 450 in SAT Math.

For the IB specifically, no points threshold for equivalency should be taken from a tutoring page, including this one. The published British-track and American-track figures above come from a named news source reporting the Ministry's clarification; the IB figure was not stated there and must be confirmed on moe.gov.ae or with the emirate's attestation authority. Al Ain families applying to United Arab Emirates University, Al Ain University or a capital institution should also read the programme's own entry requirements, which can be stricter than the equivalency floor.

sections.heading: Academic honesty: what a Physics tutor may and may not do
paragraphs: The Physics course has two components where the boundary matters: the scientific investigation and, for students who choose it, the Physics Extended Essay. Both must be the student's own work, and the school's supervisor signs an authenticity declaration. A tutor who crosses that line exposes the student to an academic misconduct finding, which is a far larger risk than a disappointing mark. Some providers in this market sell completed coursework outright, and that is an IB malpractice trigger, not a service.

What a tutor may legitimately do is substantial. Teach the technique on different data. Ask whether a research question is answerable with the equipment available. Point out that an uncertainty has been propagated inconsistently and teach the rule, so the student can find the rest themselves. Read a student's own draft and say which criterion a paragraph is failing and why. Set practice questions and mark them. All of that is teaching, and all of it is allowed.

What a tutor may not do is produce any part of the submitted work. No text, no graphs built for the student, no rewritten paragraphs returned for pasting, no suggested conclusion the student has not reached from their own data. The practical test we use with students is whether they could explain and defend every sentence to their supervisor without help. If not, it is not their work, and they should not submit it. This boundary is stated to the student in the first session, not discovered at the deadline.
bullets: Allowed: teaching technique, criterion-referenced feedback on the student's own draft, marked practice
Allowed: challenging feasibility, method and uncertainty treatment before data is collected
Not allowed: supplying text, graphs, conclusions or edits that become part of the submission

process.description: One free trial lesson per family, with no card details taken beforehand. The tutor uses it to watch the student attempt two past-paper questions aloud, which is what separates a prerequisite gap from a command-term problem. You get a written summary of what the tutor found whether or not you continue.

process.description: After the trial you receive a plan naming the topics, the number of sessions and what will be different at the end. Block bookings for a single theme or for the investigation have an explicit end date. Open-ended weekly sessions are offered only where the problem genuinely runs across the course.

process.title: Weekly notes and an honest review point
process.description: Notes go to parent and student after each session. At the review point we say whether the plan is working, and if the answer is that the student needs a different tutor or that school support is now enough, we say that instead of extending the booking.

whyPoints.title: Matched to a theme, not to a postcode
whyPoints.description: The constraint on Higher Level Physics tutoring in Al Ain is specialist supply, not distance. Online delivery means the match is made against the HL-only topic your child is stuck on rather than against who can drive to Al Muwaiji by five o'clock on a Tuesday.

whyPoints.title: The investigation treated as 20% of the grade
whyPoints.description: Most support in this market concentrates on the papers because that is what school reports describe. The scientific investigation is a fifth of the grade, marked out of 24 across four criteria, and it is the component where the student controls the conditions. We plan it early rather than rescue it late.
