sections.heading: What a live video IGCSE session actually looks like
paragraphs: Parents who have not seen one imagine a lecture on a screen, and that version would indeed be worse than a tutor in the room. A working online session looks nothing like it. The shared surface is a whiteboard both people write on, usually with a stylus, and the student's working is visible stroke by stroke rather than as a finished answer. That is the single biggest teaching advantage over a tutor reading over a shoulder: a tutor can see the exact moment a student hesitates before rearranging an equation, which is where the misconception lives.

Past papers are annotated live on screen rather than passed back and forth. The student's own work is photographed or scanned before the session and marked on screen during it, with the mark scheme beside it. For maths and physics this means every line of working is discussed in place. For written subjects it means a paragraph can be highlighted and the missing mark named where it should have appeared. The session ends with that annotated document saved and sent, which is a record the family keeps rather than a conversation that evaporates.

Some subjects suit the format unusually well. Cambridge Computer Science 0478 lives entirely on a shared screen, and watching a trace table filled in real time is better diagnosis than reading the completed table. ICT 0417 is assessed on software operations a tutor can watch directly. Mathematics is a writing-and-watching subject and translates almost perfectly. English works well because the text is on screen for both people and edits can be discussed rather than made.

The honest limits are practical. The student needs a quiet room, a stable connection, a device with a keyboard and ideally a stylus or a cheap graphics tablet for maths, and a phone camera to photograph handwritten work before the session. A younger student may need a parent nearby for the first few weeks to establish the habit. And a student who will not engage with a person in the room will not engage with one on a screen either; online delivery solves a supply problem, not a motivation problem.

sections.heading: Which IGCSE components rehearse well on screen, and which need the school
paragraphs: This is where most online tutoring pages become vague, and vagueness here costs a family money. Not every part of an IGCSE course can be rehearsed over live video, and a provider who pretends otherwise is selling something they cannot deliver. The distinction is between components assessed through written reasoning, which transfer completely, and school-based practical work, which does not.

The good news for Cambridge science candidates is that the examined practical component is usually written. Paper 6 Alternative to Practical is worth 20% of an Extended science grade and it asks candidates to read apparatus diagrams, identify controlled variables, criticise a described method, read scales, plot and interpret data and suggest improvements. All of that is written reasoning about an experiment, which is exactly what a tutor can teach on a shared screen, and the question types repeat across series, which makes it one of the most coachable components on the specification.

Where the school is irreplaceable is in the practical skills themselves, and in any centre-assessed component. A student who has never used a burette will struggle with questions about one, however well they can describe the method. Pearson Edexcel's International GCSE sciences assess practical skills inside the written papers rather than through a separate component, which shifts the same requirement into the main papers. In both cases the laboratory work belongs to the school, and a tutor's job is to make sure the student understands what they did in it.

The table sets out the position component by component. Use it to decide what to spend tutoring hours on: paying for work that cannot be done properly on screen is the clearest avoidable waste in this market, and paying for highly coachable written components is where the same money produces marks.

sections.heading: The four loss patterns, and how long each one takes
paragraphs: Everything above depends on correct diagnosis, so it is worth setting the four patterns out properly, with the signs that distinguish them. They are not personality types and a student can carry two at once, but one is usually dominant and that is the one to attack first. Getting this wrong is the single most common reason a term of tutoring produces no grade movement: a timing problem treated as a knowledge problem simply produces a better-informed student who still does not finish the paper.

A knowledge gap shows as evenly distributed low marks with blank or near-blank responses on specific topics. The fix is coverage in paper-weight order, and it is the slowest of the four because there is no shortcut to content. A command-term failure shows as long, knowledgeable answers that score two marks out of four, often with the student insisting they knew it. The fix is answer-shape work, and it is the fastest: six to eight sessions can produce a visible change because nothing new has to be learned.

A timing problem shows as a score that falls off a cliff in the last third of the paper, with the early questions answered well. The fix is a per-question time budget and a question-order strategy, and progress is measurable in completion rate within two or three weeks. An accuracy problem shows as correct method with wrong final answers: dropped minus signs, wrong units, premature rounding. The fix is a checking routine applied mechanically, which students resist and which works.

Every review session should return to this table and ask which pattern the latest marked paper shows. If the dominant pattern has not changed after five or six sessions aimed at it, the diagnosis was wrong, not the student. That is a tutor's responsibility to raise, and a parent is entitled to ask the question directly at the mid-block review.

sections.heading: How a parent checks progress when the tutor is on a screen
paragraphs: The reasonable worry about online tutoring is oversight. You cannot glance into the room and see whether work is happening, and a sixteen-year-old's account of a session is not evidence. The answer is not surveillance, it is documentation, and it should be built into the arrangement from the start rather than requested after a doubt has formed.

Three artefacts do the whole job. First, the annotated work from each session, saved and sent, so you can see what was actually marked and what was written on it. Second, a short written note after each session: what was covered, what was set, and one line on how it went. Not a report, three or four sentences. Third, marked whole papers at the review points, compared mark-by-mark with the earlier one. That comparison is the only real measure of progress, because a grade on a school report is a blunt instrument that lags by a term.

What a parent should not use as evidence is a tutor's enthusiasm, a student's mood after a session, or a percentage someone quotes without saying what it is a percentage of. No statistic should be offered to you without a number of students, a date and a method behind it, and a tutoring provider who publishes satisfaction figures or grade-improvement averages without those is publishing decoration. The same applies to any guarantee: no tutor can promise a specific outcome, and the offer is a warning sign rather than a reassurance.

The last piece of oversight is the exit conversation, which should be scheduled rather than left to drift. At the end of a planned block the tutor should state plainly whether continuing is worth it, and a good tutor will sometimes say no. Reduction or stopping is a legitimate and frequent correct answer, particularly for a student who needed technique rather than teaching and has now got it.

A three-sentence note: covered, set, how it went
Marked whole papers compared mark-by-mark at each review

sections.heading: What online tutoring will not fix, and what it costs over a term
paragraphs: A page that only lists benefits is advertising. Several things are genuinely outside what an IGCSE online tutor in Al Ain can do, and knowing them before you book is worth more than a longer list of features. Motivation is the first: a student who refuses to engage with a teacher in a classroom will not transform because a different adult appears on a screen. Tutoring works on capability, and a motivation problem needs a different conversation, often with the school.

The second is coursework. IB Gram does not write, complete or produce an Internal Assessment, Extended Essay, Theory of Knowledge essay, Personal Project or any assessed coursework, and does not edit a draft until it stops being the student's own work. A tutor teaches the skills the task assesses, explains criteria, questions a weak plan and gives written feedback on the student's own draft. A provider in this market sells completed Internal Assessments; the student who submits bought work carries the malpractice risk, not the seller.

The third is the school's own role. A tutor cannot enter your child for an exam, change a tier decision, supply laboratory experience, or alter a forecast grade. Those sit with the school, and the exams officer is the person who holds the correct zone timetable, since every Cambridge centre is allocated to one of six administrative zones and Cambridge states it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after the wrong zone timetable was used. Nor can any tutoring provider perform or guarantee Ministry of Education equivalency, which is a process the Ministry runs and which should be verified on moe.gov.ae.

On cost, the useful calculation is per block rather than per hour. Published market rates for a qualified online subject tutor run roughly AED 150 to AED 300 an hour, with specialists in thin-cohort subjects quoted higher, and monthly package pricing around AED 799 for eight online sessions has been published in this market. Multiply by the number of sessions in the plan and you have the real figure to decide on. The table does that arithmetic for the common block shapes, using published market bands rather than an IB Gram price list; our own rate is agreed after a free trial lesson and a tutor match.

process.title: Send the marked paper first
process.description: Before anything else, send one recently marked school paper with the marks still on it, plus the syllabus code and the series. That single attachment is what makes the first session a diagnosis rather than an introduction, and it is the difference between a plan and a subscription.

process.title: Take the free trial and ask for the week-one output
process.description: The trial is free and carries no obligation. At the end of it, ask for the two or three named loss points, ranked by how cheap each is to fix, and a testable prediction for the coming week. A tutor who cannot produce that from a marked paper is not the specialist for this subject.

process.title: Agree the plan, the end date and the review points
process.description: Settle how many sessions, what each phase covers, when the whole papers happen and when the two reviews fall. Fix an end date. A block that ends on a date and is renewed deliberately costs less and works better than an open-ended weekly booking nobody reassesses.

process.title: Set a slot the Al Ain school run survives
process.description: Work backwards from a normal arrival time and add thirty minutes. Central districts generally hold a 5pm or 5.30pm start; Hili, Zakher and the outlying districts are usually better from 6pm. Consistency across the term beats length, so choose the slot you can actually keep.

process.title: Review against marked papers, then decide
process.description: At the mid-block and end-block reviews, compare marked papers mark-by-mark rather than comparing impressions. If the dominant loss pattern has not moved, the plan changes. If it has closed, reducing or stopping is the correct outcome and should be said out loud.

whyPoints.title: A written plan, not an open booking
whyPoints.description: Every block starts with named loss points, a phase-by-phase plan and a defined end date, sent to the parent before any paid session. The alternative, an hour a week with no stated objective, is the default in this market and the reason so much tutoring produces nothing measurable.

whyPoints.title: Diagnosis from evidence
whyPoints.description: The first session reads a marked paper and separates knowledge gaps from command-term failure, timing and accuracy. Those four need four different interventions, and treating the wrong one is the commonest way a term of paid sessions leaves a grade exactly where it started.

whyPoints.title: Honest limits on what the format can do
whyPoints.description: Written components rehearse completely over live video; laboratory experience and centre-assessed work belong to the school. We say which is which rather than implying everything can be done on a screen, because paying for the wrong thing is the avoidable waste here.

whyPoints.title: Progress you can read
whyPoints.description: Annotated work saved and sent after each session, a three-sentence note, and marked whole papers compared at each review. No satisfaction percentages, no grade-improvement averages, no self-asserted ratings, because none of those can be checked by the person paying.

whyPoints.title: Specialists matched by syllabus code
whyPoints.description: Cambridge 0580 Extended and Pearson 4MA1 Higher are different papers. Tutors are matched to the code the Al Ain school enters for, and where a thin-cohort subject has no specialist free we say so with a realistic match time instead of placing a generalist.

whyPoints.title: Stopping is a legitimate recommendation
whyPoints.description: A planned block ends with a written recommendation, and sometimes that recommendation is to stop or to reduce. A tutor whose advice is always to continue is not reviewing the evidence, and an arrangement with no exit conversation is designed to drift.

faqs.question: How many weeks before we can tell whether online tutoring is working?
faqs.answer: Two to three weeks if the dominant problem is timing or accuracy, four to eight if it is command-term technique, and six to twelve if there are genuine content gaps. The reason for the range is that the four loss patterns move at different speeds, which is why the first session should name which one you are dealing with and predict what the next piece of work will look like. If that prediction fails, the diagnosis was wrong and the plan should change in week two rather than at the end of the block.

faqs.question: What should I receive after each online session?
faqs.answer: Three things, and they should be agreed before you pay for anything. The annotated work from the session, saved and sent, so you can see what was marked and what was written on it. A short note of three or four sentences: what was covered, what was set, and one line on how it went. And at review points, a marked whole paper compared mark-by-mark with an earlier one. That comparison is the only real measure of progress, because a school report grade lags by a term and a tutor's enthusiasm is not evidence.

faqs.question: Can a tutor teach Cambridge Paper 6 Alternative to Practical over live video?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it is one of the strongest arguments for the format. Paper 6 is worth 20% of a Cambridge Extended science grade and it tests written reasoning about experiments: reading apparatus diagrams, identifying controlled variables, criticising a described method, reading scales, plotting and interpreting data, and suggesting improvements. The question types repeat across series, which makes it unusually coachable. What a tutor cannot provide is the laboratory experience the questions assume, so the school's practical sessions still matter. Pearson candidates meet practical skills inside the written papers instead of in a separate component.

faqs.question: What equipment does my child need for online IGCSE lessons in Al Ain?
faqs.answer: A quiet room, a stable connection, a device with a proper keyboard, and headphones. For maths, physics and chemistry, a stylus or an inexpensive graphics tablet makes a real difference, because the teaching value comes from the tutor watching working appear stroke by stroke rather than reading a finished answer. A phone camera is needed to photograph handwritten school work before the session so it can be annotated live. A younger student often benefits from a parent nearby for the first few weeks while the habit forms.

faqs.question: Is it better to start tutoring in September or wait for the mock results?
faqs.answer: September, in almost every case. Starting before mocks means the mock itself becomes free evidence at the mid-block review rather than the first data point, and it means content coverage is still possible instead of triage. There is also a market reason: specialist availability in Al Ain tightens sharply in the months before a series, particularly in thin-cohort subjects like Cambridge Additional Mathematics 0606, and rates stiffen as slots disappear. Waiting for mocks usually converts a twelve-week content-and-technique plan into an eight-week technique-only one.

faqs.question: My child insists they know the material but the marks are low, so what is going on?
faqs.answer: Usually a command-term failure, which is the most common and most fixable pattern at IGCSE. The student writes a long, knowledgeable answer and scores two marks out of four because the question said explain and they described, or it asked for a comparison and they gave two separate statements. A marked paper makes this visible immediately: good content, half marks, and a student who feels unfairly treated. The fix is answer-shape work on describe, explain, suggest, compare and evaluate, and it tends to show within four to eight sessions because nothing new has to be learned.

faqs.question: How many sessions a week should an Al Ain Year 11 student have?
faqs.answer: One, in most cases, and two only in an exam-term block on a single subject. The limit is not the lesson, it is the homework, and an Al Ain Year 11 student is typically carrying eight or nine IGCSE subjects plus mandatory Arabic, social studies and Islamic studies. Two tutored subjects at once means two plans and roughly double the independent work, which is the point at which students quietly stop doing any of it. Diagnose which one or two subjects are costing the most grades, work on those, then reassess at the review.

faqs.question: Does online tutoring work for a student who is disengaged rather than struggling?
faqs.answer: Not on its own, and anyone who says otherwise is selling. Tutoring works on capability: gaps, technique, timing, accuracy. A student who will not engage with a teacher in a classroom will not engage differently because the adult is on a screen. What sometimes helps is a very short, highly structured block on one narrow component, where early visible success does the motivational work. But the conversation that actually matters in this situation usually involves the school, and a tutor who recognises that and says so is being useful rather than unhelpful.

faqs.question: What happens in the sessions during the school's mock fortnight?
faqs.answer: The mock replaces the planned content and becomes the review. There is no point teaching new material in a week when the student is sitting papers, and the mock paper itself is the most valuable document the arrangement will produce: a full-length, independently marked piece of evidence under time pressure. The session in that window is used to prepare for the specific papers being sat, and the session after it is spent reading the marked mock mark-by-mark against the week-one diagnosis. That comparison decides whether the second half of the plan stays as written.

faqs.question: How does a 14-week plan survive the Ramadan weeks in Al Ain?
faqs.answer: Move the slot after Iftar, shorten the sessions, and change what they contain. Full timed papers belong in the weeks either side; the Ramadan weeks carry consolidation, short question sets, flashcard-style recall and marking review. School hours shorten and sleep patterns shift, so a plan that pretends the month is normal produces four poor sessions and a demoralised student. Because the dates move each year, agree the revised schedule a few weeks in advance and confirm the school's adjusted timetable before fixing the new slot.

faqs.question: Can one online tutor cover both Cambridge and Pearson papers for different children?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, but ask rather than assume. Cambridge Extended sciences use a multiple-choice paper worth 30%, an extended theory paper worth 50% and Paper 6 Alternative to Practical worth 20%. Pearson 4PH1, 4CH1 and 4BI1 use two written papers with practical skills assessed inside them. Mathematics differs too: 0580 splits into Core and Extended routes with a non-calculator paper, while 4MA1 tiers into Foundation and Higher with two equally weighted papers. A tutor who has taught both can switch, but the plans stay separate because the papers reward different things.

faqs.question: What does a 14-week block actually cost at Al Ain market rates?
faqs.answer: Published market rates for a qualified online subject tutor run roughly AED 150 to AED 300 an hour, so fourteen 90-minute sessions sit somewhere between about AED 3,150 and AED 6,300 at those bands. Monthly online package pricing around AED 799 for eight sessions has also been published in this market. Those are market observations from October 2026 attributed to the providers who published them, not an IB Gram price list; our rate is agreed after a free trial lesson and a tutor match. Calculate per block rather than per hour before deciding.

faqs.question: What are the exit criteria for ending a planned block?
faqs.answer: When the dominant loss pattern has closed and marked papers show it has stayed closed across two or three attempts. That is a real and frequent outcome, particularly for students whose problem was technique rather than knowledge: once the answer shapes are learned, the work is maintenance the student can do alone. A planned block should end with a written recommendation, and a tutor who always recommends continuing is not reading the evidence. Reduction to a maintenance slot, or stopping entirely, should be on the table at every review.

faqs.question: Will an online tutor talk to my child's school in Al Ain?
faqs.answer: Not directly, and you should not expect it. A tutor is an independent party, not a member of the school's staff, and the school's communication is with you. What a tutor should do is work from the school's own documents, which you can supply: the term's scheme of work or topic list, the most recent marked assessment, and the syllabus code for each entry. The school's exams officer is also the person who holds the correct Cambridge zone timetable, since every centre is allocated to one of six administrative zones and the right version matters.

faqs.question: Does a tutor help with coursework or Internal Assessment drafts?
faqs.answer: With the student's own draft, yes: explaining criteria, questioning a weak research question, pointing at an unsupported claim, modelling a method on different data and holding a deadline schedule. Writing it, rewriting it to completion or supplying text for submission, never. A provider competing in this market sells completed Internal Assessments, and the student who submits bought work carries the malpractice consequence. Note too that most current IGCSE specifications put the marks in written papers and components such as Paper 6, so paper technique is where tutoring hours usually pay best.

al-ain/igcse-online-tutor.closingHeading: Send one marked paper and a date
al-ain/igcse-online-tutor.closingBody: To make an IGCSE online tutor in Al Ain worth the money, two things have to exist before the first paid session: a diagnosis from a real marked paper, and a count of the weeks left before the series. al-ain/igcse-tutor.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach IGCSE subjects to Al Ain families over live video, and each profile names the boards and the tiers that person has actually taught. That distinction matters more at this level than at any other, because a teacher fluent in one board's mark scheme is not automatically fluent in another's for the same subject.

intro.heading: Three questions to ask the school before you hire anyone
paragraphs: Parents searching for IGCSE support usually start with a subject and a worry. The more productive starting point is three factual questions to the school, all answerable in one email, because the answers change what any tutor should be doing. Which awarding body sets your child's papers in this subject? Is the entry Core or Extended, or in Pearson's case which tier? And what is the syllabus code printed on the specification? Until those are known, a tutor is teaching a generic version of the subject and hoping it overlaps.

The board question is the one families are most often wrong about. Al Ain schools use Cambridge International, Pearson Edexcel and in some cases OxfordAQA, and a single school may use different boards for different subjects, which is entirely normal and permitted. Cambridge mathematics is not Pearson mathematics: the papers are structured differently, the tiering works differently, and the command-term conventions differ. A tutor who teaches one well and the other from memory is a worse match than a tutor who teaches only yours.

The tier question decides the ceiling. Cambridge offers Core and Extended routes in many subjects, and the Core route is not an easier path to the same grades: it caps the highest grade available. Pearson operates its own tiering arrangements in some subjects. A student entered on the wrong route either cannot reach the grade their next step requires or is sitting papers pitched beyond their current level, and both outcomes are usually fixable in Year 10 and awkward by the middle of Year 11.

The code question sounds pedantic and is the most practical of the three. A syllabus code such as 0580 for Cambridge mathematics, 0625 for physics or 0620 for chemistry identifies exactly which specification and which component structure applies, and the board publishes the current syllabus against that code. One syllabus code appeared across the entire seven-page area cluster audited for this project, which tells you how rarely anyone else works at this level of specificity. A tutor who asks for the code in the first message is working from your child's actual syllabus.

The rest of this page works through all three decisions, then through the things that follow from them: the component structure behind each code, why the entry deadline sits months before the paper, what the Ministry of Education counts for equivalency, how practical science is handled when tuition happens over video, where marks are most reliably lost subject by subject, what comes after IGCSE for an Al Ain student, and what the market charges. IB Gram delivers tuition to Al Ain families as live one-to-one video; home visits are a service we provide only in India. Al Ain parents comparing centres also want to know which of those boards their child is actually entered for before they pay for anything, so that is where this page starts rather than where it ends.

al-ain/igcse-tutor.programmesIntro: IGCSE sits in the middle of a longer sequence, and the decision made at each end affects it. The four stages below describe what comes before, the IGCSE years themselves, and the two post-sixteen routes an Al Ain student chooses between, with notes on how each stage looks in this city's schools.

programmes.name: Lower Secondary and Checkpoint years
programmes.description: The years before IGCSE formally begins, where Cambridge schools often use Lower Secondary schemes of work and Checkpoint tests, available in March, May and October sittings. Nothing here appears on a certificate, which is exactly why it is the cheapest place to fix a problem. Algebraic fluency, scientific vocabulary and the discipline of structuring a written answer are all built or missed in these three years.
programmes.countryNote: Al Ain schools vary considerably in how much they formalise these years, and some run a British Key Stage 3 model instead. For a parent the useful question is whether the school sits Checkpoint at all, because a Checkpoint result is the last external data point before the IGCSE entry decision is made. Where a school does not sit it, the Year 9 internal reports carry that weight instead.

programmes.name: International GCSE
programmes.description: Two years of externally examined subjects, usually eight to ten of them, set by Cambridge International, Pearson Edexcel or OxfordAQA and sat in series across the year. The tier or route is chosen during this period, most of the content is taught in Year 10, and Year 11 is substantially revision and technique. Grades are the first external record a student carries, and they are what universities and the Ministry eventually look at.
programmes.countryNote: In Al Ain, British-curriculum provision is the larger part of the private-school market and IGCSE is consequently the commonest qualification in the city. Several schools run it alongside an IB Middle Years stream in the same building, so a family comparing their child's report with a neighbour's may be comparing two different assessment systems entirely.

programmes.name: AS and A Level
programmes.description: The post-sixteen continuation of the British route, with International A Levels examined by Cambridge and Pearson in their own series. Subject depth increases sharply and the number of subjects drops to three or four. The step from IGCSE Extended to AS Level in mathematics and the sciences is the one most students underestimate, because IGCSE rewards thorough coverage and A Level rewards handling unfamiliar problems.
programmes.countryNote: For an Al Ain student, the practical relevance of this route is the Ministry of Education equivalency rule for the British track, which requires one accredited subject at Advanced Level with a grade of no less than E, or two accredited subjects at Advanced Subsidiary Level with the same grade, alongside the five IGCSE or GCSE subjects. That makes the post-sixteen choice a documentation question as well as an academic one.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: The alternative post-sixteen route, with six subjects, three at Higher Level, graded one to seven, plus a core of Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and creativity, activity and service. It demands breadth where A Level demands depth, and the transition from IGCSE is smoother in some subjects than others. IGCSE Extended mathematics maps reasonably onto Standard Level; the jump to Higher Level Analysis and Approaches is substantial.
programmes.countryNote: Al Ain has considerably fewer IB World Schools than Abu Dhabi island, so a student wanting the Diploma may have a shorter list of campuses than they expect, and fewer Higher Level options running at each. Families often discover this during Year 11, which is late. The question is worth asking in Year 10, while the IGCSE subject set can still be adjusted to support either route.

al-ain/igcse-tutor.subjectsIntro: Each subject below carries its Cambridge syllabus code where one applies, with the Pearson equivalent named where Al Ain schools commonly use it. The notes say what the component structure rewards and where marks most reliably go missing, because that is the detail that tells a tutor what to teach rather than what to revise.

subjects.name: Mathematics (Cambridge 0580, Pearson 4MA1)
subjects.levels: Core and Extended, or Pearson's tiers
subjects.description: The most requested IGCSE subject in Al Ain and the one where tier choice matters most. Marks go on algebraic manipulation done at speed, on failing to show method where method carries the marks, and on misreading the demand of a multi-part question. Confirm with the school which board and which tier before any tutoring plan is built, because the papers are differently structured.

subjects.name: Additional Mathematics (Cambridge 0606)
subjects.description: Taken alongside mathematics by stronger candidates, often as preparation for A Level, and it is a genuine step up rather than an extension. Calculus, trigonometric identities and kinematics appear here. Students who cope with 0580 Extended by thorough practice rather than by understanding tend to struggle, which makes this a useful early diagnostic for A Level readiness.

subjects.name: Physics (Cambridge 0625, Pearson 4PH1)
subjects.levels: Core and Extended, or Pearson's tiers
subjects.description: Electricity is the topic Al Ain students name most often, and the quantitative treatment of waves and energy transfer costs more marks than mechanics does. The practical component exists in two forms depending on what the school enters, and knowing which one applies changes revision entirely. Formula recall and unit discipline are where marks are recovered cheaply.

subjects.name: Chemistry (Cambridge 0620)
subjects.description: Moles and reacting-mass calculations separate grades more sharply than organic chemistry does, despite students fearing the latter. Qualitative analysis tests and ionic equations reward systematic practice. The practical component, in whichever form the school enters, needs apparatus knowledge and method-writing that a theory-only revision plan never covers.

subjects.name: Biology (Cambridge 0610)
subjects.description: Content volume makes recall structure the limiting factor, and students who build their own summaries from the syllabus statements outperform those revising from exercise books. Extended-response marks go on command-term discipline, since describe, explain and suggest reward different things. Experimental-skills questions reward familiarity with variables and controls rather than content knowledge.

subjects.name: English as a First Language (Cambridge 0500)
subjects.description: Directed writing and the reading-response components reward technique that can be taught quickly, which makes this one of the better-value subjects to tutor late. Marks go on answering the question asked rather than writing well in general, and on failing to use the text as evidence. Timing in the longer components is a frequent and fixable problem.

subjects.name: Economics (Cambridge 0455)
subjects.description: Diagram accuracy and the use of data in extended answers carry the grade. Students lose marks drawing a correct diagram that does not address the question, and by describing both sides of an argument without reaching a judgement. Definitions have to be precise rather than approximate, which is a drilling job that responds well to weekly work.

subjects.name: Business Studies (Cambridge 0450)
subjects.description: Application to the case material in front of the student separates the upper bands from the middle ones. A generic answer about motivation theory earns little; the same point tied to the business in the question earns a great deal. Numerical sections, including break-even and cash flow, are where marks are most reliably added in a short tutoring block.

subjects.name: Computer Science (Cambridge 0478)
subjects.description: Theory questions on data representation, networks and system architecture carry more marks than most students expect, and are frequently neglected in favour of programming practice. Pseudocode conventions must match the board's own, which is a common and avoidable loss. A student who codes confidently can still be several grades short on the written paper.

subjects.name: Arabic as a First Language
subjects.description: Requested more often in Al Ain than in most UAE cities, and distinct from Arabic as an additional language in both content and expectation. Worth noting for equivalency purposes: Arabic and Islamic education are not included among the five required subjects for the Ministry's British-track count, so a strong grade here does not substitute for a fifth qualifying subject.

subjects.name: Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences
subjects.description: Taken instead of three separate sciences by many Al Ain students, and the specification covers all three disciplines in less depth with a different paper structure. A tutor needs to know which variant the school entered, because preparing a combined-science candidate with separate-science material wastes a substantial share of every session.

sections.heading: Which board sets your child's papers
paragraphs: This is the first question and the one most often answered wrongly at home. Al Ain schools use Cambridge International, Pearson Edexcel and in some cases OxfordAQA, and there is no requirement that a school use one board for everything. A student can sit Cambridge sciences and Pearson mathematics in the same year, which is normal and is frequently not communicated clearly to parents.

The differences are not cosmetic. The papers are structured differently, the tiering arrangements differ, the command-term conventions differ, and the published mark schemes reward different things in an extended answer. A tutor teaching Cambridge conventions to a Pearson candidate will produce answers that read well and score less than they should, which is an expensive and entirely avoidable error.

Cambridge also does something no other board in this market does, and it catches families out. It allocates every examination centre to one of six administrative zones, states that it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for your zone, and warns that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after using the wrong one. A timetable found through a search result may belong to a different zone entirely. Get the zone and the timetable version from the school, in writing. The entry details are on the statement of entry the school issues each series, and they name the board, the syllabus code and the tier in one place. Reading that single document settles the question faster than any conversation with a tuition centre, and it is the document to have open before the first session is booked.

sections.heading: Core or Extended: the decision that sets the ceiling
paragraphs: Cambridge offers Core and Extended routes in many IGCSE subjects, and the distinction is routinely misunderstood as easier and harder versions of the same thing. It is not. Core covers less of the syllabus, is examined on different papers, and caps the highest grade a candidate can be awarded. A student entered on Core cannot reach the top grades however well they perform, which is a fact worth knowing in Year 10 rather than in the spring of Year 11.

Entry on the wrong route damages in both directions. A capable student placed on Core is held below the grade their next step needs, and may find a sixth-form or Diploma place conditional on something they were never able to achieve. A struggling student placed on Extended sits papers pitched beyond their current level and often performs worse than they would have on Core, where the content is more securely within reach.

The decision is the school's, taken on evidence, and it is usually reviewable earlier in the course than families assume. The useful parental move is to ask two questions in Year 10: which route is my child currently entered on, and what would need to be true for that to change? Teachers answer that specifically. A tutor's contribution is an honest view on whether the gap between the two routes can be closed in the time available, and roughly how many hours that would take. The school makes that entry decision, but a parent is entitled to ask which tier the child sits on and why.

sections.heading: The syllabus code and what sits behind it
paragraphs: A syllabus code is the most useful six characters in an IGCSE conversation. Cambridge mathematics is 0580, physics is 0625, chemistry is 0620, biology is 0610, English as a first language is 0500, economics is 0455, business studies is 0450, computer science is 0478 and additional mathematics is 0606. Pearson uses its own codes, such as 4MA1 for mathematics and 4PH1 for physics. The code identifies the exact specification, which is published by the board and which states the current component structure and weightings.

Why it matters practically: specifications are revised, and a tutor working from a version two revisions old will teach content that has moved or been removed. Asking for the code and then reading the board's current syllabus against it takes ten minutes and eliminates that whole class of error. It also settles the practical-component question in the sciences, because which component a school enters is specified rather than assumed.

We deliberately do not publish component weightings here. They are set by the board per specification, they change, and reproducing a board's syllabus document is not something we do. The correct move is to read the current syllabus for your child's code on the board's own site, and that is also the answer a tutor should give when asked. A provider who quotes weightings off a page without naming the code and the version is quoting something that may no longer be true. A centre that cannot name the code is guessing at the content, and in Al Ain that is worth checking before you pay.

sections.heading: Why the entry closes months before the paper
paragraphs: Almost every family is surprised by this, and the surprise is expensive when it concerns a retake or an additional subject. Entries close long before the examination itself, and the school or centre has its own internal deadline ahead of the board's. Because IGCSE boards publish their dates, this can be shown with real figures rather than described in general terms.

Take Cambridge's March 2027 series as the worked example. The board's published key dates put the examination period at 3 February to 4 March 2027, with final entries due on 27 November 2026, forecast grades due on 27 February 2027, results released on Direct on 13 May 2027 and certificates issued in late June. The entry therefore closes more than two months before the first paper is sat, and the decision about tier and subject has to be made before that. Pearson runs International GCSE series in May and June and in November, published its November 2026 final timetable running from late October to 19 November 2026, and sent June 2026 results to centres on 19 August 2026 and to students the following day, with November 2025 results reaching students on 22 January 2026.

Pearson also publishes provisional timetables ahead of each series, which is why a tutoring plan should link the live official timetable rather than restate dates that can be revised. For an Al Ain family the procedural steps are short: ask the school who holds entry responsibility, ask for the school's internal entry deadline, ask which series and which tier your child is entered for, and get all three in writing. Then build the revision plan backwards from the examination window rather than from the end of term.

sections.heading: What the Ministry of Education counts
paragraphs: Equivalency is the reason IGCSE grades matter beyond school, and it is a subject almost nobody competing for these searches covers. For the British track, the published requirement is that a student passes five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates with a grade of no less than E or grade three, and submits proof of one accredited subject at Advanced Level with a grade of no less than E, or two accredited subjects at Advanced Subsidiary Level with the same grade.

Two details inside that rule matter to Al Ain families specifically. Arabic and Islamic education are not included among the five required subjects, which surprises households where those are strong grades and which means the five has to be made up from other qualifications. And the figure is five: one page currently ranking for these searches states that UAE candidates must take six IGCSE subjects, which does not match the sourced requirement. Publishing the correct number is more useful than publishing a confident one.

For completeness, the American-track requirement published alongside it asks for English proficiency evidenced by a score of 5 in the IELTS academic test, 61 in the TOEFL internet-based test, or 450 in the reading and writing section of the SAT, and mathematics evidenced by at least 450 in the SAT mathematics test. No IB points threshold for equivalency has been read on the Ministry's own pages, so none is published here. Equivalency is a process families complete through the Ministry's own channel. It is not something IB Gram performs, guarantees or is required for, and no part of it depends on tutoring.

sections.heading: Practical science when the tuition happens over video
paragraphs: This is the honest limitation and it deserves a section rather than a footnote. A tutor working over live video cannot run an experiment with your child. What a tutor can do is everything around the experiment, and in IGCSE science that is where most of the marks sit.

The practical component in the Cambridge sciences exists in more than one form depending on what the school enters, and the first job is finding out which one applies to your child's code. Where a written alternative to the practical is sat, the question types are entirely teachable remotely: identifying variables and controls, reading a method for flaws, completing results tables with correct significant figures, plotting and interpreting graphs, calculating gradients, and writing a conclusion that refers to the data rather than to the expected result. Those are skills, and they respond to practice.

Where a laboratory practical test is sat, the experiment happens at school and the tutor's job is apparatus knowledge, method discipline and the write-up conventions the mark scheme rewards. Either way, the practical skills component is the part of IGCSE science most often neglected in revision, because it is the hardest part to revise from a textbook. That makes it one of the better uses of tutoring time rather than a reason to avoid tutoring, provided nobody pretends the experiment itself can be done through a screen. The alternative-to-practical paper rewards reading a method and a results table rather than holding a pipette, which is exactly the skill a shared screen trains well.

sections.heading: After IGCSE in Al Ain: the Year 11 decision
paragraphs: IGCSE results arrive as a set, and the set opens or closes doors. In Al Ain the post-sixteen options are a British sixth form taking International A Levels, an IB World School taking the Diploma, or a move to a campus outside the city for either. The city's IB school count is lower than Abu Dhabi island's, which means the Diploma route can involve a shorter list of campuses and fewer Higher Level options running at each.

The subject-mapping question is where tutoring decisions in Year 10 and 11 start to matter. IGCSE Extended mathematics maps reasonably onto Diploma Standard Level mathematics or onto an A Level with support; the step to Higher Level Analysis and Approaches is substantially larger and is the commonest place a confident IGCSE student struggles in the first Diploma term. Separate sciences map more comfortably onto A Level and Higher Level sciences than combined science does, which is worth knowing before the Year 10 option forms are submitted.

The practical sequence for a family is short. Ask the intended sixth form or Diploma school, in Year 10, what grades and which subjects it requires. Check whether the route your child is entered on, Core or Extended, can deliver those grades. Then decide what the following eighteen months need to contain. Doing this in Year 10 keeps every option open; doing it after results arrive narrows the choice to whatever is still available in late August.

sections.heading: What IGCSE tuition costs in this market
paragraphs: Three of the six competitor pages audited for this project publish no price at all, and the two that do quote in a currency UAE families do not transact in. The figures below are what other providers publish in dirhams, with the provider type attached. They are market context rather than our price list, and IB Gram's own figure is set at consultation after the trial lesson.

The spread is wide and the reason is mostly format rather than quality. Budget online rates begin around AED 45 to 65 with one provider and AED 33 to 52 with another, typically for university-student tutors. A qualified subject tutor working online is published from AED 150 for IGCSE by one agency. In-home visiting rates run AED 180 to 350 in one 2026 Dubai rate table and AED 200 to 500 from independent home tutors, with travel inside the figure. Specialist rates are quoted at AED 270 by one UK-based agency and AED 200 to 450 and above elsewhere, and one premium provider publishes AED 650.

Monthly packages are also published in this market: around AED 799 a month for eight online sessions, and AED 1,599 to 1,799 a month for four two-hour in-home sessions. For a weekly one-hour arrangement, one rate-comparison source estimates AED 240 to 600 a month at the budget end, AED 600 to 1,200 in the middle and AED 1,000 to 2,000 and above for specialist exam-year support. Read all of this against the two-year shape of IGCSE: Year 10 content work at the ordinary band costs less in total than Year 11 crisis work at the specialist band, and buys more.

process.title: Email the school the three questions
process.description: Which board, which tier or route, and which syllabus code, subject by subject. One email, usually answered in a day, and it changes what any tutor should be teaching. Families who skip this step routinely pay for several sessions aimed at the wrong specification before anyone notices.

process.title: Send us the code and a marked paper
process.description: The syllabus code tells a tutor which specification to read; a recent marked paper shows where the marks actually went. Those two documents together are worth more than a long description of the problem, and they let the first session start with a diagnosis rather than an introduction.

process.title: Confirm the series and the entry deadline
process.description: Ask the school which series your child is entered for and what the school's own internal entry deadline is. For a retake or an additional subject this is the binding constraint, because entries close more than two months before the paper and the plan has to be built backwards from that.

process.title: Trial the match before paying
process.description: One lesson at no charge, one per family, with no card details taken beforehand. It runs as a working session: the tutor identifies something specific against the syllabus, teaches a piece of it, and sets out what the next six weeks would contain. If the match is wrong, we change the tutor rather than asking the student to adapt.

process.title: Set the slot against the real arrival time
process.description: Not the school finish, the hour your child is genuinely home and able to concentrate, which from Zakher, Hili or Al Foah is after six. Hold the first choice for a fortnight before moving it. A slot that survives into the spring term is worth more than one that looked neat in September.

whyPoints.title: Board and tier established first
whyPoints.description: Nothing is planned until we know which board sets the papers, which route the student is entered on and which syllabus code applies. A tutor fluent in Cambridge conventions teaching a Pearson candidate produces answers that read well and score less, and that error is entirely avoidable in one email.

whyPoints.title: Dates taken from the boards themselves
whyPoints.description: Every date on this page comes from Cambridge International's or Pearson's own published material and is attributed to it. No date is restated as fact where a board publishes it only provisionally, and the live official timetable is where a family should confirm anything that matters.

whyPoints.title: Equivalency explained, not performed
whyPoints.description: The Ministry's published British-track requirement is five accredited subjects at no less than grade E or grade three, excluding Arabic and Islamic education, plus the post-sixteen layer. We explain it and point to the official channel. IB Gram does not perform, guarantee or expedite equivalency, and tutoring is not required for it.

whyPoints.title: Honest about practical science
whyPoints.description: A tutor over video cannot run an experiment. We teach the alternative-to-practical question types, graph and significant-figure work, variable identification and write-up conventions, which is where most of the recoverable marks are, and we say plainly that the experiment itself happens at school.

whyPoints.title: Rates published with their sources
whyPoints.description: Three of six audited competitor pages publish no price at all. Every AED band on this page is attributed to the provider type that published it, in dirhams rather than dollars, and presented as market context. Our own figure is set at consultation, after the trial lesson.

whyPoints.title: No status we do not hold
whyPoints.description: IB Gram holds no approval, accreditation, licence or partnership from Cambridge, Pearson, OxfordAQA, ADEK, the Ministry of Education or the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation. We explain what those bodies do and never imply that any of them endorses us.

faqs.question: Is my child sitting Cambridge IGCSE or Pearson Edexcel International GCSE?
faqs.answer: Ask the school, subject by subject, because the answer can differ between subjects in the same timetable and frequently does. Al Ain schools use Cambridge International, Pearson Edexcel and in some cases OxfordAQA, and nothing obliges a school to use one board for everything. The difference matters because the papers are structured differently, the tiering arrangements differ and the published mark schemes reward different things in extended answers. A tutor teaching the wrong board's conventions produces answers that read well and score below their potential, which is the most avoidable loss in the whole qualification.

faqs.question: What is the difference between Core and Extended in Cambridge IGCSE?
faqs.answer: Core covers a reduced subset of the syllabus, is examined on different components and caps the highest grade available. Extended covers the full specification and keeps the whole grade range open. They are not easier and harder versions of one paper set, which is the common misunderstanding. A capable student placed on Core can be held below the grade their sixth form or Diploma school requires, and a struggling student placed on Extended often performs worse than they would have on Core. Ask the school which route your child is entered on and what would need to change for that to move.

faqs.question: Can my child move from Core to Extended partway through Year 11?
faqs.answer: The decision belongs to the school and depends on how much of the Extended content remains untaught, which is why the question is far easier to answer in Year 10. Earlier in the course a move is usually possible with a term of concentrated work. By the spring of Year 11 the hours rarely exist, because Extended requires additional taught content rather than simply more practice on the same material. The useful parental question is not whether a move is allowed but how many taught hours the gap represents, and a tutor can give an honest estimate of that after a diagnostic session.

faqs.question: How many IGCSE passes does the Ministry of Education need to see for equivalency?
faqs.answer: For the British track, the published requirement is five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates with a grade of no less than E or grade three, together with proof of one accredited subject at Advanced Level at no less than E, or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade. One page currently ranking for these searches states that UAE candidates must take six IGCSE subjects, which does not match the sourced requirement. Verify the current position on the Ministry's own pages before acting, because the process belongs to the Ministry rather than to any tutoring provider.

faqs.question: Are Arabic and Islamic Education included in the five subjects?
faqs.answer: No. The published rule states that Arabic and Islamic education are not included among the five required subjects for the GCSE or IGCSE count. That surprises Al Ain households where those are among the strongest grades, and it has a practical consequence: the five qualifying subjects have to be made up from other qualifications entirely. It is worth checking the full subject set against this rule in Year 10 rather than after results, because the fix at that stage is simply an option-form adjustment rather than an additional entry in a later series.

faqs.question: When do IGCSE entries close relative to the exam itself?
faqs.answer: Much earlier than most families expect, and the school's own internal deadline sits ahead of the board's. Cambridge's published key dates for its March 2027 series put final entries on 27 November 2026 against an examination period of 3 February to 4 March 2027, so the entry closes more than two months before the first paper. Pearson publishes its own series dates and issues provisional timetables ahead of each one. For a retake or an additional subject this is the binding constraint on the whole plan, so ask the school for its internal entry deadline in writing.

faqs.question: Which IGCSE series do Al Ain schools normally enter?
faqs.answer: Most enter the main summer series, with November used for retakes and for individual subjects. Cambridge International runs IGCSE, O Level and International A Level examinations in a June series and a November series, with a March series available in some regions, and its Primary and Lower Secondary Checkpoint tests sit in March, May and October. Pearson Edexcel runs International GCSE in May and June and in November. Which series applies to your child is a question for the school rather than something to infer, because entry decisions are made per subject and per candidate.

faqs.question: What does the syllabus code on my child's paper mean?
faqs.answer: It identifies the exact specification, which is what determines the component structure, the content and the practical arrangements. Cambridge mathematics is 0580, physics 0625, chemistry 0620, biology 0610, English as a first language 0500, economics 0455, business studies 0450, computer science 0478 and additional mathematics 0606. Pearson uses codes such as 4MA1 and 4PH1. The code matters because specifications are revised, and a tutor working from an older version teaches content that has moved or gone. Ask the school for it and read the board's current syllabus against it.

faqs.question: If lessons are online, how does my child's IGCSE science practical get assessed?
faqs.answer: By the school, through whichever practical component the syllabus code specifies, which may be a laboratory test or a written alternative. A tutor working over video cannot run the experiment and we do not suggest otherwise. What a tutor can teach is everything around it, and that is where the marks mostly sit: identifying variables and controls, spotting flaws in a method, completing results tables to the right significant figures, plotting and interpreting graphs, calculating gradients, and writing conclusions that refer to the data. These are the most neglected marks in IGCSE science revision.

faqs.question: Where do IGCSE maths candidates lose the most marks?
faqs.answer: In three predictable places. First, method marks not shown, because a correct answer with no working scores less than the question offers. Second, speed of algebraic manipulation, which costs time rather than marks directly and then costs marks at the end of the paper. Third, misreading the demand of multi-part questions, particularly where a later part depends on an earlier result. None of those is a content gap, which is why a student who seems to know the material can still underperform, and all three respond quickly to timed practice marked against the board's own published mark scheme.

faqs.question: Is Year 10 or Year 11 the better time to start IGCSE tutoring?
faqs.answer: Year 10, by a wide margin, because most of the syllabus is taught then and an hour spent keeping content level is worth several spent recovering it. Year 10 work also sits at the ordinary market band rather than the specialist exam-year band, so the same budget buys more weeks. Year 11 tutoring is technique, timed papers and targeted repair, and it works well when the content is broadly in place. Where half a specification is missing in the spring of Year 11, the honest conversation is about triage rather than about buying more hours.

faqs.question: What IGCSE tutoring rates do providers in Al Ain publish?
faqs.answer: The published spread is wide. Budget online rates begin around AED 33 to 65 with platforms using university-student tutors. A qualified subject tutor working online is published from AED 150 for IGCSE by one agency, with the band running to roughly AED 300. In-home visiting rates run AED 180 to 350 in one 2026 Dubai rate table and AED 200 to 500 from independent home tutors, travel included. Specialists are quoted from AED 200 to 450 and above, and one premium provider publishes AED 650. These are other providers' published figures, not IB Gram's prices.

faqs.question: Can my child take different IGCSE subjects with different boards?
faqs.answer: Yes, and many Al Ain students already do without the family realising it. Schools choose a board per subject, so Cambridge sciences alongside Pearson mathematics is an ordinary arrangement. The implication for tutoring is that the board question has to be asked subject by subject rather than once. The implication for revision is that past papers, mark schemes and command-term conventions have to be drawn from the right board for each subject, and mixing them is one of the quieter ways a well-prepared student loses marks.

faqs.question: What happens after IGCSE for an Al Ain student choosing between DP and A-Levels?
faqs.answer: A Levels narrow to three or four subjects with greater depth; the Diploma keeps six with a core of Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and creativity, activity and service. The practical constraint in Al Ain is supply: the city has considerably fewer IB World Schools than Abu Dhabi island, so the Diploma route may mean a shorter list of campuses and fewer Higher Level options at each. Ask the intended sixth form or Diploma school in Year 10 what grades and subjects it requires, then check whether the route your child is entered on can deliver them.

faqs.question: How many IGCSE subjects should my child have tutoring in at once?
faqs.answer: One or two, almost always. A student taking nine or ten subjects has limited independent study time, and three or four tutored subjects consume the hours in which the rest of the work has to happen. The better pattern is to fix the weakest subject properly, then move the hour to the next one, rather than running four shallow arrangements in parallel. The exception is the final term, where two subjects at two sessions a week is manageable if both are technique work rather than content repair.

faqs.question: Can a resit improve an IGCSE grade, and when would it be sat?
faqs.answer: Resits are possible and are usually taken in a later series, which for Cambridge means the November series or a March series where available, and for Pearson the November series. The constraint is the entry deadline rather than the preparation: entries close well before the paper, and a school or centre has its own internal deadline ahead of the board's. Decide early, confirm who is making the entry, and get the series and tier in writing. The entry itself is always made by the school or an approved examination centre rather than by a tutoring provider.

al-ain/igcse-tutor.closingHeading: Send one email before you book anything
al-ain/igcse-tutor.closingBody: The highest-value thing you can do this week is not hiring a tutor. It is sending one email to the school asking, subject by subject, which board sets the papers, which route or tier your child is entered on, and which syllabus code applies. Those three answers determine what any tutor should be teaching, and they are usually returned within a day. Bring them to the trial lesson, which runs at no charge, one per family, with no card details taken first, along with one recently marked paper. With the code and the paper in hand, the first session can start with a diagnosis against your child's actual specification instead of a conversation about it.

intro.heading: A map pin is the wrong filter for an IGCSE problem
paragraphs: A search for an IGCSE tutor near me in Al Ain is a search sorted by distance. That is a sensible filter for a plumber and a poor one for a Cambridge Chemistry 0620 Extended candidate, because the thing that decides whether the hours work is whether the tutor has taught that specification through a series, and geography has no relationship to that at all. The result a parent gets is a list of whoever is closest and most visible, which in a city the size of Al Ain is a short and semi-random list.

Do the arithmetic and the problem becomes obvious. Al Ain's private-school set is considerably smaller than Abu Dhabi island's, and far smaller than Dubai's, where 387,441 students attended 227 private schools across 17 curricula in 2024-25. Fewer schools means fewer cohorts, and a subject with four or five candidates a year per school produces a very small number of teachers in the whole city who have taught it. For Cambridge Additional Mathematics 0606, Further Pure Mathematics 4PM1 or Computer Science 0478, the honest count of local specialists is low enough that distance-first searching will often return nobody suitable and several people willing.

Proximity does buy real things, and this page is not going to pretend otherwise. A person in the room can watch a younger student's attention wander and act on it. Handwriting, calculator habits and the physical business of laying out a maths answer are easier to correct beside someone. A household that wants visible supervision gets it. Those are genuine, and for some Al Ain families they outweigh everything else. The question worth asking is not whether proximity has value, but what you are paying for it in specification match.

The cost shows up in three places. It shows up in the AED rate, since published UAE in-home one-to-one figures run roughly AED 180 to AED 500 an hour with travel included, against roughly AED 150 to AED 300 for a qualified subject tutor working online. It shows up in scheduling, because a tutor driving from central Al Ain to Al Yahar or Al Maqam has to leave before they know if the previous lesson overran. And it shows up in the shortlist, which narrows from everyone qualified to everyone nearby and available.

IB Gram's position is stated rather than implied: there are no home visits anywhere in the UAE and no office, centre or branch in the country, because in-home tutoring is a service offered only in India. Al Ain families are taught one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time. That is not a claim that screens beat rooms. It is a claim that in a city this size, choosing by syllabus code beats choosing by driving distance, and that a family in Zakher should be able to work with whoever has actually taught 0606 rather than whoever is twelve minutes away.

al-ain/igcse-tutor-near-me.programmesIntro: Which option is right depends partly on what stage the student is at, because the value of proximity falls as the subject gets more specialised. These are the four stages and what each one changes about the search.

programmes.name: Key Stage 3 and Cambridge Lower Secondary
programmes.description: The stage where proximity is worth the most, because the work is general, the student is young, and supervision matters more than specification depth. Any competent maths or English teacher can close a Year 8 gap. Checkpoint tests run in March, May and October and are diagnostic rather than certificated, which makes this a low-pressure stage to intervene in.
programmes.countryNote: In Al Ain this is also the stage to find out what the school will actually offer at IGCSE. Narrower option blocks than on Abu Dhabi island mean a subject your child wants may run as a very small group or not at all, and Year 9 is when that is still fixable without changing school.

programmes.name: Year 10, the first IGCSE year
programmes.description: Specification experience starts to matter more than proximity. A tutor needs to know whether the entry is Cambridge 0580 Core or Extended, or Pearson 4MA1 Foundation or Higher, because the papers differ and so does the working the mark scheme rewards. A generalist can still help, but the gap between a generalist and a specialist opens here.
programmes.countryNote: Al Ain families often discover mid-Year 10 that their child is being taught Core and Extended content in the same room, with differentiation left to worksheets. That is the most common reason a local search starts, and it is a specification problem rather than a proximity problem.

programmes.name: Year 11, the examined year
programmes.description: Proximity is now worth least and specification match worth most. The work is paper technique against a known mark scheme: command terms, timing, and the two or three question types the student reliably drops. A tutor who has not marked against the board's own scheme cannot see which word was missing from an answer that scored two of three.
programmes.countryNote: Availability in Al Ain tightens sharply in the ten weeks before a series, and so does the market. A distance-first search in April returns whoever still has slots, which is the weakest possible selection criterion at the point when selection matters most.

programmes.name: AS, A Level and the Diploma Programme
programmes.description: At this level the local pool thins to almost nothing for most subjects. A Higher Level Diploma science or an A Level further maths tutor is a specialist job, and the number of people in Al Ain who have taught the current specification is small. Distance-based searching at this stage reliably produces a mismatch.
programmes.countryNote: Al Ain offers fewer Diploma Programme places than Abu Dhabi island, so students wanting a particular Higher Level combination sometimes commute or change school. Planning that from Year 10, with the IGCSE grades it needs, is far cheaper than discovering it in Year 11.

al-ain/igcse-tutor-near-me.subjectsIntro: The honest answer to a local search varies enormously by subject. These are the IGCSE subjects Al Ain families search for, and what the local supply position actually looks like in each.

subjects.name: Mathematics (Cambridge 0580, Edexcel 4MA1)
subjects.levels: Core and Extended; Foundation and Higher tier
subjects.description: The one subject where a local search usually works, because the pool is the largest in the city. Even here, ask which route and tier the tutor has taught: 0580 requires a non-calculator paper and 4MA1 does not tier the same way.

subjects.name: Additional Mathematics (Cambridge 0606), Further Pure (Edexcel 4PM1)
subjects.description: The thinnest local pool of any IGCSE subject in Al Ain. Cohorts of a handful per school mean very few teachers in the city have taken it through a series. A distance-first search here reliably returns a willing generalist rather than a specialist.

subjects.name: Physics (Cambridge 0625, Edexcel 4PH1)
subjects.levels: Core and Extended; Foundation and Higher
subjects.description: Reasonable local supply at Core level, thinner at Extended. Ask specifically about Paper 6 Alternative to Practical, which is 20% of a Cambridge Extended grade and which many general science tutors have never taught as a component.

subjects.name: Chemistry (Cambridge 0620, Edexcel 4CH1)
subjects.levels: Core and Extended; Foundation and Higher
subjects.description: Similar local picture to Physics. The subject contains three separate problems, moles calculations, qualitative analysis and organic patterns, and a tutor strong on one is not automatically strong on the others. Ask which they teach most often.

subjects.name: Biology (Cambridge 0610, Edexcel 4BI1)
subjects.levels: Core and Extended; Foundation and Higher
subjects.description: The best-supplied science locally, and the one where general teaching helps least. Most lost marks are command-term failures rather than knowledge gaps, which needs someone who reads mark schemes rather than someone who knows biology.

subjects.name: Coordinated Sciences (Cambridge 0654)
subjects.description: Widely taught in Al Ain because triple science blocks are small, and widely misunderstood by tutors who prepare candidates with single-science papers. Ask directly whether they have taught 0654 rather than 0625, 0620 or 0610.

subjects.name: English as a Second Language (Cambridge 0510, 0511)
subjects.description: Good local supply and a subject where proximity genuinely helps younger students. The exercises are predictable and unforgiving about following instructions, so marked timed practice matters more than the teaching venue.

subjects.name: First Language English (Cambridge 0500, Edexcel 4EA1)
subjects.description: Reasonable local supply, variable quality. The test is whether the tutor talks about the mark scheme split between structure and expression, or about reading more widely. Only one of those answers earns marks in June.

subjects.name: Computer Science and ICT (Cambridge 0478, 0417)
subjects.description: Thin locally, and the two subjects are routinely confused with each other. Computer Science needs pseudocode and trace tables; ICT needs timed software technique. Ask which code, then ask what they have taught, in that order.

subjects.name: Business Studies and Economics (Cambridge 0450, 0455)
subjects.description: Moderate local supply. The useful skill is case-study technique and reaching the evaluation mark at the end of a long question, which is where most candidates stop. General business knowledge does not substitute for it.

subjects.name: Arabic as a First and as an Additional Language (Cambridge 0508, 0544)
subjects.levels: First language and foreign language routes
subjects.description: Local supply exists but is often matched by subject name rather than by route. These are separate specifications with separate demands, and a first-language tutor teaching a foreign-language candidate is the common mismatch.

subjects.name: Geography and History (Cambridge 0460, 0470)
subjects.description: Thin locally at IGCSE level. Both are source-handling and structured-recall subjects where the loss is structural: students answer the question they revised rather than the one printed. Essay planning under time is the intervention.

al-ain/igcse-tutor-near-me.regionsIntro: In a city as spread out as Al Ain, near me means something different in each district. These are the areas families search from and what the local answer realistically looks like.

regions.name: Al Jimi
regions.note: The densest part of the city and the one place where a distance-first search returns a reasonable list, because several long-established campuses sit close by. Even so, the list is of nearby tutors, not of tutors who teach your syllabus code.

regions.name: Al Mutaredh and Al Khabisi
regions.note: Central-west districts with mixed curriculum catchments. Households here often have two children at different schools on different boards, which is precisely the situation a single nearby tutor cannot usually cover.

regions.name: Falaj Hazza and Al Muwaiji
regions.note: Established villa districts west of the centre. The drive from the central school belt is short enough that local arrangements work, and long enough that a travel premium appears in the rate without being itemised.

regions.name: Hili and Al Qattara
regions.note: Northern districts with longer bus routes, so children arrive home late and local tutors arrive later. A near-me search here tends to return a shorter list than the same search in Al Jimi, for no reason other than density.

regions.name: Al Towayya and Asharej
regions.note: Close to the university quarter, so the nearby pool includes a high proportion of university students. That is a legitimate budget-tier option for Year 9 and Year 10 support and a weak one for an Extended exam-year subject.

regions.name: Zakher
regions.note: A spread-out southern district where local supply thins quickly for specialist subjects. Families here are the most likely to find that the nearest suitable tutor is not near at all, which is where the online shortlist does its work.

regions.name: Al Maqam and Al Yahar
regions.note: The outlying districts. A tutor's round trip from the centre can exceed the lesson, so a local search returns either a very small list or a rate that quietly prices the journey. A no-journey slot from 4.30pm is the practical alternative.

regions.name: Al Foah and Al Sarooj
regions.note: Northern and central districts with fewer private-school catchments nearby. A near-me search returns few results, and the useful response is to widen the filter from distance to specification rather than to accept the nearest option.

schoolClusters.city: British-curriculum campuses across Al Ain
schoolClusters.note: These schools run IGCSE into AS and A Level or into the Diploma Programme. Their option blocks are narrower than on Abu Dhabi island, which has a direct effect on local tutor supply: a subject taught to five candidates a year produces almost no local teaching pool over time. This is the structural reason a near-me search works for maths and fails for Additional Mathematics.

schoolClusters.note: Larger cohorts, so a larger local pool in maths and the sciences, and a steady flow of students moving onto an IGCSE track part-way through. For a transition student the first weeks of any arrangement go on question style rather than content, which is a specification skill and not something proximity supplies.

modes.description: One session a week against the school's current topic, which is the format that compounds and the one least likely to produce a spring crisis. The practical advantage over a local arrangement is that the slot does not move when traffic, weather or a previous lesson overruns, so the student's week has a fixed point in it rather than a probable one.
